Name: action_prior_imprinting
Title: Majority-Action Bias in Retrieved Agent Memory: A Query-Independent Action Prior, and Why Removing It Requires Per-Retrieval Calibration
Short Hypothesis: Injected agent experience influences behaviour through two separable channels: a query-dependent channel (this item tells the agent what to do *here*) and a query-independent channel in which the empirical action/tool histogram of the injected block is copied onto the agent's action prior irrespective of the current state. We hypothesise the second channel is large, is the dominant source of memory-induced breakage in sequential agents, and — because retrieval makes the injected histogram change from query to query — can only be removed by a *per-retrieval* estimate of it. The falsifiable consequence is a double dissociation: subtracting the per-block query-independent component beats (a) scalar context scaling (CFG/CAD), which can only amplify or attenuate both channels together, and (b) a fixed global bank base-rate offset, which is what classic ICL calibration reduces to when the demonstration set is static.
Related Work:
Zhao et al. (ICML 2021, "Calibrate Before Use") identified majority-label and recency bias in classification ICL and removed it with a content-free probe; Batch Calibration (Zhou et al. 2023), Prototypical Calibration (Han et al. 2022) and Domain-Context Calibration (Fei et al., ACL 2023) refine the bias estimate. We concede up front, as both reviewers demanded, that the *mechanism* (demonstration frequency imprints a prior; a probe can estimate and subtract it) is four years old and not our contribution. Two structural facts distinguish the agentic setting and define what is actually new here. First, in classic ICL the demonstration set is **fixed across the evaluation**, so a single global offset — one probe, one correction — suffices, and no prior calibration paper has had to answer whether adaptivity buys anything. Under retrieval the injected block, and therefore the induced prior, changes at every query and every step; whether per-retrieval estimation beats a fixed bank-level offset is an open empirical question and is now one of our two headline predictions. Second, the biased quantity is a tool/action choice inside an episode, where a single mis-selection ends or derails the trajectory, so the same per-decision bias compounds rather than costing one label.

On the agent side, ExpeL (AAAI 2024), Agent Workflow Memory (ICML 2025), Synapse and ReasoningBank-style systems inject retrieved trajectories and report end-to-end gains; diagnostic work attributes memory failures to "irrelevant retrieval". Our own pilot is the direct antecedent: a retrieved bank fixed zero held-out items and broke six to seven (McNemar p=0.031, replicated), injection *volume* rather than content was the causal lever, and call-balance rebalancing neutralised the harm while the retrieved items were topically correct throughout. A relevance account does not explain that; an action-marginal imprinting account predicts it exactly. Note that the rebalancing result already implies action-mix imbalance matters — so "imbalance matters" is *not* claimed as novel either.

Context-aware decoding (Shi et al., NAACL 2024) and CFG for LMs (Sanchez et al. 2023) contrast with-context and without-context logits but scale the entire contextual influence by one coefficient. Our claim is a factorisation: memory's influence splits into a harmful query-independent part and a useful query-dependent part, so a scalar on the whole thing is the wrong instrument. Prompt optimizers (MIPRO, GEPA) can in principle fix an imbalanced demonstration slot by search; we treat that as a named competitor and as the coupling link to the track.

Stated narrowly, the new objects are: (i) a causal, action-mix-controlled test of imprinting in a *sequential* agent with relevance, length and correctness held fixed, including a topically-irrelevant mix-matched control that fixes the boundary condition; (ii) a probe *validated before use* against synthetic blocks with known marginals and against an in-distribution real-state-averaged estimator; (iii) the adaptivity dissociation (per-retrieval vs global offset) that classic ICL calibration could not pose; (iv) the factorisation-vs-scaling head-to-head; (v) what an imprinting-biased memory does to a prompt optimizer running on top of it.
Abstract:
Agentic memory systems retrieve past trajectories and inject them into the prompt, and are reported to help; controlled measurement instead shows they can fix zero held-out items and break six to seven, with injection *volume* rather than content as the causal lever. We propose a mechanism that explains this and yields a cheap fix. Retrieved blocks are not action-neutral: the trajectories a retriever returns have an action histogram, and we hypothesise the agent copies this histogram onto its action prior largely independently of the current state. This is the sequential-decision analogue of majority-label bias in in-context learning, with one difference that carries the science: because the block is retrieved per query, the induced prior moves from step to step, so — unlike the static-demonstration setting where a single global correction suffices — removing it should require a *per-retrieval* estimate.

We test imprinting causally by holding topical relevance, token count and ground-truth correctness fixed while manipulating the action mix of the injected block, adding a mix-matched but topically irrelevant block to fix whether imprinting needs plausible content. We validate a state-marginal probe against synthetic blocks with *known* action marginals and against an in-distribution real-state-averaged estimator, and only then use it to subtract the query-independent component at decision time (marginal action calibration, MAC). The confirmatory claim is a double dissociation on a sequential domain: MAC should beat best-tuned CFG/CAD (which cannot separate channels) *and* beat a fixed bank-level base-rate offset (which cannot track per-retrieval drift), while zero-cost instruction debiasing and action-balanced retrieval are carried in the same grid as live competitors. ALFWorld with 1,000 paired held-out games is the power-bearing testbed (paired MDE ≈ 3 points); a 1,500-instance annotated tool-selection benchmark is demoted to a cheap cross-model generality check and the venue for a GEPA optimizer-coupling experiment. Total budget: ≈45 GPU-node-hours on 4×A100 and ≈$150 of API.
Experiments:
**Agent and scoring.** ReAct-style agent with an enumerable action set. At each decision step every admissible action string *a* is scored by length-normalised log-probability under the current prompt (vLLM, prefix caching), giving a distribution over the admissible set; all analyses use this distribution and the executed argmax. Decoding is greedy, so an episode is deterministic given the environment seed and prompt; residual nondeterminism (batching/kernel) is measured, not assumed away (see Measurement).

**Testbeds. ALFWorld is now the power-bearing testbed, per reviewer instruction.**
- **ALFWorld (sequential; carries the headline claim).** Memory distilled from 500 training games. Confirmatory evaluation on **1,000 disjoint held-out training games** (in-distribution, paired, identical initial states across conditions); tuning/screening on a further disjoint 200-game validation split; the 134-game standard *unseen* split is used only as an explicitly under-powered directional shift check. ~25 admissible actions/step, ~30 steps/episode.
- **Tool selection (demoted to cheap generality + optimizer venue).** BFCL-v3-style single-turn function selection, 1,500 held-out annotated instances, ~20–60 candidate tools. It no longer carries the factorisation claim; it carries the cross-model/action-space-size check and the GEPA coupling experiment, both of which are single-decision and near-free.
- **WebShop remains cut.**

**Models.** Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is the only model on ALFWorld. Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct appear only on the single-turn tool benchmark, at a reduced 3-condition grid, and carry the scale/family scoping claim (P9) — which is explicitly scoped to single-turn.

**E0 — Gate and descriptive skew (cheap).** Confirm memory injection moves ALFWorld success beyond the measured noise floor in either direction. Per state, compute the verb histogram of the retrieved top-4 block, its JSD from the bank marginal, and the step-to-step drift of that histogram within an episode (the quantity that makes adaptivity plausible). Report the fraction of states with a usable equal-relevance substitution pool. If retrieved blocks are already action-neutral, or if the per-block histogram never departs from the bank marginal, there is nothing to imprint and nothing for adaptivity to buy; we report a bounded null and stop.

**E1 — Causal test of imprinting, with a relevance boundary control (core mechanism experiment).** For 1,500 ALFWorld held-out decision states and 1,000 tool instances, build four injected blocks matched within 5% on token count (and, for the first three, on mean retrieval score) but differing in the share of a target action *v*:
- LOW (~0), MID (~0.25), HIGH (~0.6), constructed by substituting items from the equal-relevance band of the ranking;
- **IRR-HIGH** (new, R1's missing baseline): share of *v* ≈ 0.6, same token count, but items drawn from topically *irrelevant* memory entries (bottom-decile retrieval score). This separates "imprinting is a token-level frequency effect" from "imprinting requires plausible, relevant content", which is exactly the boundary CFG proponents will push on.
Measure P(choose *v*), log-odds of *v*, and whether the executed action was correct (ALFWorld: expert-plan-admissible; tool: gold API). Analysis: mixed-effects logistic regression of choose(*v*) on injected share of *v*, with state/episode random intercepts and fixed effects for whether *v* is correct at that state, retrieval score, block length; the design decorrelates share from correctness by construction. 3 independent substitution draws.
Runs: (1,500 + 1,000) states × 4 conditions × 3 draws = 30,000 scored decisions, plus 2,500 no-block scorings.

**E2 — Probe validation (gate; runs before MAC is used anywhere).**
(a) *Recovery of a known marginal.* 40 synthetic blocks with designed verb histograms (target share 0/0.25/0.6, token count fixed). The content-free probe (goal → "N/A", observation → template listing the same admissible actions, same injected block) must recover the designed marginal: Spearman ρ ≥ 0.7 between designed share and probe-estimated log-odds shift.
(b) *Out-of-sample predictive validity.* Probe-estimated bias must predict the mean memory-induced logit shift on *held-out real states* carrying that block (out-of-sample R², not in-sample fit).
(c) *OOD-artifact control.* Compare against a **real-state-averaged estimator** (mean logit shift over 20 random real states carrying the same block; in-distribution by construction, content-marginalised). Correlation ≥ 0.8 rules out "the probe measures OOD prompting weirdness"; disagreement means MAC uses the real-state-averaged estimator and the content-free probe is reported as invalid for agents.
Runs: 40 blocks × (3 probe variants + 20 real states) ≈ 920 block-state scorings.

**E3 — Factorisation and drift.** Across real states sharing a block, regress δ(a,s) = log p(a|block,s) − log p(a|no block,s) on the probe shift; report R² (query-independent share) and residual (query-dependent share), over 3 probe designs. Additionally regress δ on the *global bank* base-rate shift alone; the gap between the two R² values is the direct in-silico prediction of how much adaptivity is worth, and is measured before the expensive confirmatory run. Reuses E1/E2 scorings.

**E4 — Screening on the validation split (ALFWorld, 200 games).** Tune γ for CFG/CAD over 5 values, λ for MAC over 3 values (competitor deliberately given the finer grid), and evaluate the four cheap competitors: k=2 volume reduction, instruction-level debiasing, action-balanced retrieval, **global bank base-rate offset** (R2's missing baseline — a fixed, non-adaptive offset equal to the bank-wide action log-marginal). Output: γ*, λ*, and the single strongest zero-cost competitor, all fixed before touching held-out data.
Runs: 12 configs × 200 games = 2,400 episodes.

**E5 — Confirmatory grid (ALFWorld, 1,000 held-out games; this decides the paper).** Five conditions: (i) no memory; (ii) uncalibrated k=4; (iii) **MAC at λ\***; (iv) **CFG/CAD at γ\***; (v) **global bank base-rate offset** (kept in the confirmatory grid regardless of screening, because P4 is a headline prediction). Plus the screening-winning zero-cost fix if it differs from (v), as a sixth condition on a 500-game subset.
Primary outcome: episode success rate, paired McNemar against condition (ii) and head-to-head MAC vs CFG and MAC vs global offset. Pre-registered secondary, higher-power outcomes on the same runs: step-level executed-action correctness (~30,000 paired steps) and first-error step index.
Runs: 5 × 1,000 + 1 × 500 = 5,500 episodes.

**E6 — Shift check and noise floor.** Unseen-134 split, 4 conditions × 134 = 536 episodes (directional only, MDE ≈ 8 pts, no claim made). Noise floor: 2 configurations re-run twice on 250 games = 1,000 episodes, plus a null replicate in which one configuration is relabelled a "treatment" and compared against itself.

**E7 — Where the harm lives.** Paired fix/break decomposition vs no-memory, stratified by whether the state's correct action was over- or under-represented in the injected block relative to its base rate. Prediction: breaks concentrate in the under-represented stratum; MAC removes most of them without removing fixes in the over-represented stratum. No new runs (analysis of E5).

**E8 — Coupling with prompt optimization (track fit; on the cheap single-turn testbed).** GEPA-style reflective instruction optimization (frontier model as reflector) under a fixed budget of 300 metric rollouts on a 300-instance validation split, three times: (a) against uncalibrated injected memory; (b) against MAC-calibrated scoring; (c) with the optimizer instead searching over *which* items to inject (k and a verb-balance constraint) — an optimizer-based competitor to MAC. Evaluate all evolved artifacts on the 1,500-instance held-out set with paired fix/break decomposition against their own starting prompt. Evolved instruction deltas are classified for verbal anti-bias content ("consider all tools equally") as a cheap read on whether the optimizer spends budget fighting imprinting.
Runs: 3 × 300 search + 3 × 1,500 held-out = 5,400 single-turn decisions, ~150 reflection API calls.

**E9 — Cross-model generality (tool benchmark, single-turn).** 7B at 5 conditions (no-mem, uncalibrated, MAC, CFG@γ*, global offset) × 1,500; 14B and Llama-3.1-8B at 3 conditions (uncalibrated, MAC, CFG@γ*) × 1,500. This is a generality check, not the headline.
Runs: 7,500 + 4,500 + 4,500 = 16,500 single decisions, plus 300×9 = 2,700 tuning decisions.

**Compute arithmetic (hard envelope: 4×A100 80GB, days not weeks, few hundred $ API).**
- ALFWorld episodes: memory build 500 + screening 2,400 + confirmatory 5,500 + shift 536 + noise floor 1,000 ≈ **9,940 episodes × ~30 steps ≈ 298,000 decision steps**. Each step = one ~3.5k-token prefill (prefix-cached within episode) plus ~25 short scoring continuations. Pilot throughput with 4 data-parallel 7B vLLM replicas and continuous batching: ≈6 decision-steps/s aggregate → ≈13.8 h. With a 3× safety factor for throughput overestimation: **≤42 h**.
- Step-level mechanism runs (E1–E3): ≈33,400 scored decisions, no rollouts → **≤3 h**.
- Tool benchmark (E8 + E9, three models): ≈24,600 single decisions at ~1.5k-token prompts → **≤4 h** (14B accounts for ≤2 h).
- **Total ≈ 49 GPU-node-hours ≈ 2 days wall clock** on the single node, inside the "days, not weeks" envelope with headroom.
- Frontier API: memory distillation (~500 ALFWorld + ~500 tool training episodes → ~1,000 summarisation calls) + ~150 GEPA reflection calls; no LLM judging (env reward / gold labels throughout). **≈ $120–150.**
Baselines and Ablations:
**Baselines that could plausibly win (all live, none decorative).**
1. **CFG / context-aware decoding at best-tuned γ*** — the decisive scaling competitor, tuned on a finer grid than λ. If it ties MAC within the noise floor, the factorisation claim fails and the honest conclusion is "just down-weight the whole memory context". Pre-committed.
2. **Global bank base-rate offset** (added at R2's request) — a fixed, query-independent correction using the bank-wide action marginal, no per-retrieval forward pass. This is what classic ICL calibration degenerates to when demonstrations are static. If it ties MAC, per-retrieval adaptivity buys nothing and the contribution reduces to "Calibrate Before Use applies to agents", which we will say in those words.
3. **Instruction-level debiasing** — zero-cost prompt telling the agent to ignore demonstration action frequency.
4. **Action-balanced retrieval** — greedy top-k selection matching the bank's verb marginal; retrieval-side, no log-probs.
5. **GEPA-selected demonstrations** (E8c) — an optimizer given a matched budget to choose/reweight injected items.
6. **Volume reduction k=2** — the pilot-validated cheap neutraliser. MAC must produce *gain*, not merely absence of harm.
7. **No memory** — the floor.

**Ablations (five; each isolates one mechanism step).**
(a) *Substitution control*: replace items with different items of the same action mix and equal relevance — imprinting predicts no shift (isolates histogram from item identity).
(b) *Relevance boundary*: IRR-HIGH block from E1 — mix-matched, topically irrelevant. Prices whether imprinting is a pure token-frequency effect.
(c) *Probe design*: content-free "N/A" goal vs empty observation vs in-distribution real-state-averaged estimator — prices the OOD risk and supplies a fallback.
(d) *λ sweep* {0, 0.5, 1.0}; λ=0 recovers uncalibrated injection.
(e) *Free estimator*: calibrate using the block's literal action histogram (no forward pass at all). If this ties the probe, the probe is not worth its cost and we report that.

**Cut ablations and why:** length-matched neutral padding (subsumed by IRR-HIGH, which is length-matched and mix-matched), first-action-only calibration, artificial action-space resizing (replaced by the natural ALFWorld-vs-tool contrast), success-only vs mixed memory, retrieval-score thresholding. None decides the main claim.
Falsifiable Predictions:
**P0 (the probe is valid; gate, tested before use).** Probe-estimated bias recovers designed action marginals with Spearman ρ ≥ 0.7, achieves out-of-sample R² ≥ 0.3 predicting real-state logit shifts, and correlates ≥ 0.8 with the in-distribution real-state-averaged estimator. *Refutation:* any failure ⇒ the content-free probe is an OOD artifact; MAC falls back to the real-state-averaged estimator and the failure is reported explicitly.

**P1 (imprinting exists, is causal, and is largely content-independent).** In E1 the imprinting coefficient's 95% CI excludes zero and a 10-point increase in an action's share raises its odds of execution by ≥15%, controlling for correctness. The topically-irrelevant mix-matched block (IRR-HIGH) reproduces ≥50% of the shift produced by the relevant HIGH block. *Refutation:* coefficient indistinguishable from zero ⇒ hypothesis dead. If IRR-HIGH reproduces <25%, imprinting is content-gated rather than a pure frequency effect and we rewrite the mechanism claim accordingly (MAC still applies, but the analogy to majority-label bias is weakened and we say so).

**P2 (large query-independent component).** The probe explains ≥40% of variance in memory-induced logit shift across states sharing a block. *Refutation:* R² < 0.15 ⇒ memory's influence is essentially state-specific and there is nothing marginal to subtract.

**P3 (factorisation beats scaling) — primary confirmatory test, sized to the sample.** On ALFWorld held-out (n=1,000 paired, McNemar MDE ≈ 3.0 pts) MAC beats best-tuned CFG by **≥4 points episode success**, and beats it on step-level executed-action correctness (n≈30,000 paired steps, MDE ≈ 0.9 pts) by ≥2 points. CFG's success-vs-γ curve is single-peaked with peak below MAC. *Refutation:* CFG at γ* ties or wins within the noise floor — pre-committed to be reported as parity, in which case the contribution reduces to the validated mechanism measurement plus a demonstration that the channels are not separable in practice.

**P4 (adaptivity is necessary) — the second confirmatory test and the novelty-bearing one.** MAC beats the fixed global bank base-rate offset by **≥4 points** on ALFWorld episode success and ≥2.5 points on the tool benchmark, and E3 shows the per-block probe explains ≥15 percentage points more logit-shift variance than the bank marginal alone. *Refutation:* parity ⇒ a static offset suffices, per-retrieval estimation is unnecessary, and the honest headline becomes "classic contextual calibration transfers unchanged to agent memory" — a smaller but publishable negative-for-us result that we pre-commit to reporting as the title claim.

**P5 (MAC beats the zero-cost fixes).** MAC beats instruction-level debiasing, action-balanced retrieval, and GEPA-selected demonstrations, each by more than the relevant MDE. *Refutation:* any tie ⇒ the cheap fix suffices and MAC is not worth its forward pass; reported as the headline if it occurs.

**P6 (harm is directional in the predicted stratum).** Uncalibrated injection breaks ≥2× as many items where the correct action was under-represented as where it was over-represented (McNemar p<0.05 on the break-count difference); MAC removes ≥50% of under-represented-stratum breaks while retaining ≥70% of over-represented-stratum fixes.

**P7 (substitution control).** Swapping items for equally relevant items with the same histogram shifts the executed-action distribution by <1/3 of the shift produced by the action-mix manipulation. *Refutation:* parity ⇒ item identity, not action mix, drives the shift.

**P8 (optimizer coupling).** With uncalibrated memory, a fixed GEPA budget yields redistribution rather than gain (|fixes − breaks| below the MDE, matching the pilot's redistribution finding); with MAC the same budget yields net gain ≥2.5 points. *Refutation:* equal gains in both settings ⇒ imprinting is not a bottleneck for prompt optimization and the coupling framing is unsupported.

**P9 (scope, single-turn only).** On the tool benchmark, imprinting magnitude is larger than on ALFWorld (larger action space), and at 14B is at least half its 7B value. If it vanishes at 14B or on Llama-3.1-8B, we scope the claim to small Qwen-family models in the title. No scale claim is made for the sequential domain.
Measurement and Noise Control:
Mechanism and system claims are measured at different granularities on purpose.

*Mechanism (P0–P2, P7)* is tested on decision steps: 1,500 ALFWorld states + 1,000 tool instances × 4 action-mix conditions × 3 substitution draws, all paired (identical states and prompts except the manipulated block; greedy scoring, deterministic given the prompt). Analysis: mixed-effects logistic regression with state and episode random intercepts and cluster-robust SEs. At this sample size an odds ratio of 1.10 per 10-point share change is detectable at 80% power, below the predicted 1.15 — P1 is not underpowered.

*System (P3–P6, P8)* is tested on the noisy unit, and the power-bearing unit is now the sequential one. ALFWorld held-out: n=1,000 paired games with identical initial environment states across conditions; expected discordant proportion ≈0.25 ⇒ **McNemar MDE ≈ 3.0 points**, so P3/P4 are stated at ≥4 points. Pre-registered secondary step-level outcome: ≈30,000 paired decision steps, discordant proportion ≈0.15 ⇒ MDE ≈ 0.9 points; this is where the compounding-error story is measured (first-error step index, per-step correctness) at high power. Tool benchmark: n=1,500 paired, MDE ≈2.1 points; it supports generality and P8 only. The 134-game unseen split has MDE ≈8 points, is explicitly under-powered, and no effect is claimed on it.

Determinism and replication: decoding is greedy and environments are seeded, so episode-level variance comes only from batching nondeterminism. We measure it rather than assume it away: two configurations are re-run twice on 250 games, and one configuration is relabelled a "treatment" and compared against itself, giving the apparent effect produced by nothing. **No claim is made unless it exceeds the 95th percentile of that null distribution** in addition to being statistically significant — the same discipline that killed a positive result in the pilot. E1 uses 3 substitution draws and E2/E3 use 3 probe designs; differences must exceed twice the relevant between-replicate SD.

Hyperparameters: γ, λ, k, and the choice of strongest zero-cost competitor are fixed on the disjoint 200-game validation split (300 instances on the tool benchmark) and never touched again. γ is swept over 5 values against λ's 3, favouring the competitor.

Pre-registered primary tests, in order: (1) probe validity P0, gating everything downstream; (2) imprinting coefficient P1; (3) probe R² P2; (4) MAC vs CFG@γ* on ALFWorld episode success; (5) MAC vs global base-rate offset on ALFWorld episode success. All other contrasts Holm-corrected. Failing P0 is pre-committed to convert the paper into a mechanism-plus-negative-calibration result rather than being quietly dropped; failing P4 is pre-committed to convert the headline into "static ICL calibration transfers unchanged".
Preprint Collision Check:
**The literature search run for this proposal failed again, for the second consecutive round.** Every attempt returned "Server tool use limit exceeded"; **zero results were returned**, for batched and single queries alike covering "majority label bias in-context learning", "agent memory retrieval action prior", "query-independent bias injected demonstrations LLM agent". This is a tooling failure, not a finding. **I therefore have no verified closest recent work and no verified gap, and I will not treat silence as evidence of novelty.** Both reviewers correctly scored this as an unresolved novelty threat; it remains unresolved.

What I can name is *established, indexed* prior work known independently of this search — Zhao et al. 2021 (Calibrate Before Use) and the calibration successors, Sanchez et al. 2023 (CFG), Shi et al. 2024 (CAD), ExpeL (AAAI 2024), AWM (ICML 2025) — all listed in Related Work. Against these, the differentiators are the sequential-agent causal test with a relevance boundary control, the validated probe, the per-retrieval-vs-global adaptivity dissociation, and the optimizer-coupling measurement. I have **not** verified that no 2025–2026 preprint pre-empts these.

Unverified collision risks I consider materially likely, flagged rather than hidden: (i) frequency/majority bias in LLM function-calling or tool selection; (ii) calibrated or contrastive decoding applied to agentic memory; (iii) retrieval-induced action drift in memory-augmented agents. These are the obvious low-hanging extensions of Calibrate Before Use and at least one probably exists.

Pre-committed action before any submission, with exact queries: "majority label bias tool selection LLM agent"; "contextual calibration function calling bias"; "retrieved demonstrations action distribution bias agent memory"; "context-aware decoding agent tool choice"; "in-context demonstration frequency bias sequential decision making"; "agent memory negative transfer calibration"; "per-query calibration retrieval augmented in-context learning"; plus citation-forward sweeps of Zhao et al. 2021 and Shi et al. 2024 restricted to 2025–2026, and a citation-forward sweep of ExpeL and AWM.

Pre-committed responses if a collision is found. (a) If a preprint already demonstrates action-frequency imprinting in agents: P1 drops to a replication and the paper re-centres on P0/P3/P4 (probe validation, factorisation-vs-scaling, and the adaptivity dissociation), which no calibration paper we know of tests. (b) If a preprint already does probe-based calibration for single-turn tool selection: we say plainly in the abstract that the single-turn case is prior work, delete the tool-benchmark accuracy framing entirely, and stand on the ALFWorld sequential evidence (step-level compounding, first-error-step, stratified fix/break) plus E8. (c) If a preprint already establishes per-retrieval calibration under RAG-style variable demonstrations, the novelty claim collapses to the agentic/sequential transfer and we report it as such, at reduced ambition, rather than restating it as new.
Risk Factors and Limitations:
1. **Probe invalidity** remains the largest technical risk and is gated by E2/P0 before MAC is used. Fallback is the real-state-averaged estimator (in-distribution by construction); if both fail, the paper is a negative result about probe-based calibration for agents, retaining E1's imprinting measurement and E5's comparison of cheap fixes.
2. **CFG may tie.** It is simpler and strong. Parity is pre-committed to be reported as parity; the contribution then shrinks to a validated mechanism plus evidence that the channels are not separable in practice. We refuse to hedge this by inflating the number of measured quantities until something is significant.
3. **The global base-rate offset may tie**, i.e. adaptivity buys nothing. This is the single most damaging outcome for novelty, which is exactly why it is a headline pre-registered test rather than an appendix ablation. E3's variance decomposition gives an early, cheap read on it before the confirmatory run.
4. **Zero-cost baselines may win.** An explicit debiasing instruction or verb-balanced retrieval matching MAC makes the decode-time machinery pointless; reported as the headline if it occurs.
5. **Unresolved collision risk.** The novelty search has failed twice. The proposal is written so that its value degrades gracefully under each collision scenario (see Preprint Collision Check), but a reviewer is entitled to treat this as an open threat until the search runs.
6. **Substitution-pool coverage.** Equal-relevance items with the required action mix may not exist for many states. E0 measures this first; E1 restricts to states with a sufficient pool and reports the coverage fraction and the resulting external-validity limit.
7. **Method scope.** MAC needs token-level log-probabilities over an enumerable action set; it does not apply to free-form generative agents or closed API models. Hard scope limit.
8. **Over-correction.** Calibration may convert genuine fixes into breaks where memory's recommendation is right; E7's stratified analysis exposes this and λ<1 is the honest compromise.
9. **ALFWorld held-out games are in-distribution with the memory bank** (drawn from the training pool, disjoint from bank-construction games). This is what buys n=1,000. The unseen-134 split is the only true distribution-shift evidence and is under-powered; we state that generalisation under shift is unresolved rather than implied.
10. **Single-model sequential evidence.** ALFWorld runs 7B only; scale and family checks live on the single-turn benchmark. We do not claim the sequential result generalises across model scale.
11. **Cost.** The probe adds one forward pass per distinct injected block, amortised across steps using that block. We report amortised overhead and will not claim a free lunch if it exceeds the cost of simply reducing k — ablation (e) prices a zero-forward-pass histogram estimator against it.

Name: allocation_prior_transfer
Title: What Actually Transfers Is the Noise Model: Cross-Task Priors on Candidate Quality Make Reflective Prompt Optimization Sample-Efficient
Short Hypothesis: In reflective prompt optimizers (GEPA/MIPROv2), most rollouts are spent *evaluating* proposed candidates, not proposing them. The domain-general, transferable component of an optimization run is not the prompt or its instruction skeleton but the nuisance statistics of the search: the base rate rho at which reflection-proposed edits are genuine improvements and the effect-size distribution of those improvements. These statistics are far more similar across domains than the prompts are; a prior over them, harvested from source-domain runs, turns fixed-minibatch evaluation into sequential accept/reject testing and should beat cold-start optimization at small rollout budgets while converging to it at large budgets. If rho and the effect-size scale are strongly task-idiosyncratic, the hypothesis is refuted and cheap online estimation on the target should suffice.
Related Work: (All citations unverified; literature search was unavailable.) GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2025) evaluates each reflective mutation on a fixed minibatch and maintains a Pareto front over validation instances; MIPROv2 (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024) uses TPE over instruction/demonstration candidates with fixed-size minibatch evaluation; OPRO and APE re-score a fixed batch per candidate. All spend evaluation budget by a hand-set schedule, and all restart per task. Racing and bandit methods (Hoeffding races, irace, Successive Halving/Hyperband) adapt evaluation budget within a run but assume no cross-task prior and are typically uninformative at the start, which is exactly where prompt-optimization budgets live. Meta/transfer Bayesian optimization (e.g., transfer surrogates, ranking-weighted GP ensembles) transfers across tasks but requires a shared, low-dimensional, parametric search space; prompt text has no such shared parameterization across domains, which is precisely why prompt-optimization transfer has focused on transferring artifacts (SPoT/ATTEMPT soft prompts; instruction induction; skeleton warm starts). PromptBreeder evolves mutation operators but only within one run. Our claim is a conceptual dissociation none of these make: the search space does not transfer, but the *nuisance statistics over the search* do, and transferring them is model- and domain-portable because they are two scalars plus a shape, not text. We also test this head-to-head against textual transfer (skeleton warm start, harvested reflection heuristics) at matched budget, and test whether the two compose.
Abstract: Reflective prompt optimizers restart from scratch on every new task, and prior attempts at transfer have moved text: an optimized prompt, an instruction skeleton, a set of reflection heuristics. We argue the most reliably transferable object is statistical rather than textual. In any GEPA/MIPRO-style run, the optimizer repeatedly asks 'is this proposed candidate better than its parent?' and answers it by spending rollouts on a fixed-size minibatch. The efficiency of that answer is governed by two quantities: rho, the fraction of LLM-proposed edits that are true improvements, and the distribution of improvement magnitudes. We show these quantities are substantially more stable across domains than prompts are, and we exploit them: we fit a hierarchical prior over (rho, effect size) from optimization runs on source tasks, then, on held-out target domains, replace fixed-minibatch evaluation with a sequential accept/reject test that uses the transferred prior as its starting belief while leaving the proposal and selection machinery untouched. Because the transferred object is three numbers, it is trivially portable across executor models and APIs. We evaluate on six held-out target tasks (multi-hop QA, symbolic reasoning, code, instruction following) with 7B-32B open-weight executors, against cold-start GEPA, uninformative racing, online-estimated priors, an oracle target-fit prior, and textual-transfer baselines. The claim is Pareto and falsifiable: gains concentrated at small budgets, vanishing by convergence, with a crossover budget reported as a bootstrap interval. We additionally report the validation-to-test selection gap, predicting that principled sequential testing reduces the winner's curse that inflates all reported prompt-optimization gains.
Experiments:
(1) Noise-floor and null-replicate calibration. Re-score 20 fixed candidate prompts on the same held-out set 5x per task; measure metric SD. Run two cold-start GEPA runs differing only in seed to bound the apparent 'gain' obtainable from nothing. All later thresholds and 'null' declarations reference this floor.
(2) Source harvesting and the central measurement. Run a reimplemented GEPA (executor Qwen2.5-7B/32B local; reflector = frontier API model) on 6 source tasks (BBH clusters, Super-NaturalInstructions clusters, 2WikiMultiHop), 300 rollouts x 3 seeds. For every proposed candidate, additionally score it on a large held-out probe set (400 examples) to obtain a near-ground-truth delta vs parent. This yields, per task, the empirical distribution of true deltas: rho = P(delta>0) and the positive-part effect-size distribution. Report between-task vs within-task variance of rho and effect scale (ICC), plus leave-one-task-out predictive log-likelihood of a pooled hierarchical prior against (a) an uninformative prior and (b) the task's own oracle fit. This test alone decides the hypothesis independent of downstream gains.
(3) Method (TAP: Transferred Allocation Prior). Keep GEPA's proposal, reflection, and Pareto selection exactly as is. Replace fixed-minibatch candidate evaluation with sequential evaluation: after each block of 4 examples, compute the posterior P(delta>0) under a spike-and-slab prior (spike weight 1-rho, slab = fitted effect-size distribution) with a binomial/normal likelihood; accept if P>tau_a, reject if P<tau_r, else continue up to a cap. rho and the slab are set by the leave-one-domain-out pooled prior; nothing else changes.
(4) Target evaluation. 6 held-out target tasks (HotpotQA, GSM8K, MBPP/HumanEval+, an instruction-following set, 2 unseen BBH clusters) x 5 seeds. Budget checkpoints at 25/50/100/200/300 rollouts on both a rollout axis and a token axis; at each checkpoint report test accuracy of the current validation-argmax candidate, AUC of the budget-accuracy curve, and the crossover budget with bootstrap CI.
(5) Mechanism decomposition. Separate three possible sources of gain: (a) fewer rollouts wasted on doomed candidates (measure mean rollouts spent per rejected candidate), (b) more candidates proposed per budget (count), (c) fewer false accepts polluting the Pareto pool (measure precision of accept decisions against probe-set ground truth).
(6) Composition and head-to-head with textual transfer. Run skeleton warm start and a harvested reflection-heuristic playbook alone, TAP alone, and both together; test additivity (interaction term in the mixed model).
(7) Negative-transfer probe. Fit the prior from a single distant source domain (symbolic only) and apply to code and QA; predict TAP degrades gracefully (bounded by uninformative racing) whereas skeleton warm start can go negative.
Baselines and Ablations:
Baselines: (i) cold-start GEPA with its default fixed minibatch at matched rollouts (main competitor; wins at large budget by construction); (ii) MIPROv2 cold start; (iii) uninformative racing / Successive Halving with the same sequential machinery but a flat prior - isolates the value of *transfer* from the value of *adaptivity*, and is the baseline most likely to erase the contribution; (iv) online prior: identical to TAP but rho and effect scale estimated from the target run's own first K=15 candidates (the cheap alternative that could win outright; TAP is only interesting if it wins before this warms up); (v) oracle prior fit on the target's full probe-set deltas (upper bound); (vi) skeleton warm start and (vii) reflection-heuristic playbook as textual-transfer references.
Ablations: transfer rho only vs effect-size distribution only vs both; single-source vs six-source pooled prior; tau_a/tau_r sensitivity; block size; cap on per-candidate examples; TAP grafted onto MIPROv2 instead of GEPA (does the mechanism transfer across optimizers?); second executor model (Llama-3.1-8B) at reduced seeds to test model-portability of the transferred scalars.
Falsifiable Predictions: If the hypothesis holds: (a) between-task ICC of rho is low (pooled prior's leave-one-task-out predictive log-likelihood beats the uninformative prior by a clear margin and comes within ~10% of the oracle fit); (b) at 50 rollouts TAP beats cold-start GEPA by 2-5 test points averaged over 6 targets (paired per seed) and beats uninformative racing by 1-3 points, with both gaps shrinking below the noise floor by 300 rollouts; crossover budget 100-250 rollouts with a bootstrap CI narrower than the checkpoint spacing; (c) TAP beats the online-prior baseline over roughly the first 40-60 rollouts and ties thereafter; (d) validation-to-test selection gap shrinks by >=30% relative under TAP; (e) mechanism: >=60% of the gain traceable to rollouts saved on rejected candidates, not to accept precision; (f) TAP never underperforms cold-start by more than the noise floor even from a distant single source, while skeleton warm start loses 2-5 points on distant pairs. Refutation: rho and effect scale vary strongly by task (high ICC, pooled prior no better than uninformative); or uninformative racing matches TAP at all budgets (adaptivity, not transfer, is the whole story); or the online-prior baseline matches TAP from rollout 1; or gains are within the null-replicate floor.
Measurement and Noise Control: Four-way split per task: feedback set (traces for reflection), validation set (candidate selection inside the optimizer), a large probe set used only offline to establish near-ground-truth deltas for prior fitting and accept-precision analysis, and a never-touched test set for reporting. All methods share seeds, splits, executor model and decode settings, and reflector temperature/seed; the reflection proposal stream is *replayed identically* across evaluation-policy conditions where possible, so the arms differ only in allocation (a strictly paired design that removes proposal randomness). 6 targets x 5 seeds = 30 paired observations per comparison; analysis by paired bootstrap over (task, seed) plus a linear mixed model with task random effects and budget as a factor. With per-run test SD ~3 points measured in step 1 and n=30 paired, the design detects a 1.5-point mean paired difference at 80% power; any effect below the treatment-free null-replicate floor is reported as null regardless of p-value. We report the validation-to-test selection gap explicitly for every arm so winner's-curse inflation is quantified rather than hidden, and crossover budgets are always reported as bootstrap intervals.
Risk Factors and Limitations: (1) For binary metrics, per-example variance is analytic, so only rho and the effect-size shape are genuinely transferable; if these turn out to be near-universal, the contribution becomes 'use a sensible fixed prior' - still useful but weaker, and we would report it as such. (2) The online-prior baseline may warm up within ~10 candidates, compressing the transfer advantage to a very small budget window; we pre-register this window as the crossover measurement rather than claiming a global win. (3) Probe-set deltas are themselves noisy; we use 400 examples and report probe-set SD alongside all prior fits. (4) Six target tasks is a narrow basis for 'domain' claims; conclusions will be stated at the level of the specific task clusters. (5) GEPA's Pareto-front machinery interacts with accept/reject in ways that may not isolate cleanly; the MIPROv2 graft is included to check the mechanism is not optimizer-specific. (6) Frontier-model reflection is nondeterministic and rate-limited; capping reflection calls (~30/run) limits the number of harvested candidates per task.

Name: breadth_routed_memory
Title: Consolidate the Broad, Retrieve the Narrow: Coverage — Not Utility, Not Usage — Decides Where Agent Experience Should Live
Short Hypothesis: Whether a distilled agent-experience item should be written into the always-on instruction or left in a retrieval-gated bank is determined by its *coverage breadth* — the fraction of the deployment query distribution for which it enters the top-k — and not by its utility (how much it helps when it fires) nor by its historical usage frequency (how often it was retrieved in past traffic). Broad items occupy scarce top-k slots on nearly every episode and crowd out narrow items that would have helped the few queries they match; consolidating broad items into the instruction frees those slots. The prediction that separates this from classical caching is inverted: a hit-rate-maximizing cache promotes broad items *into* the fast tier to serve them faster, whereas we claim the value of promotion is that it *removes* the broad item from the competitive tier. Therefore a breadth-routed hybrid beats both pure always-on playbooks and pure top-k retrieval at a matched token budget, the gain arrives through narrow items newly entering the top-k rather than through the consolidated text, breadth beats usage-frequency routing exactly when past traffic is skewed relative to deployment traffic, and the effect shrinks when the retrieval mechanism does not enforce a fixed slot count.
Related Work:
Three literatures converge on this decision and none of them has run the experiment.

**(i) Always-on evolving context.** Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun et al., 2025) and agentic-context-engineering / playbook methods maintain one growing block of distilled experience present in every prompt. They never ask which items deserve permanent residency.

**(ii) Retrieval-gated episodic memory.** ExpeL (AAAI 2024), Agent Workflow Memory (ICML 2025), Synapse, and ReasoningBank-style 2025/26 systems key a bank on the query and inject a fixed top-k. They never ask which items should be promoted out of the bank. On the optimizer side, MIPROv2 (EMNLP 2024) jointly optimizes an instruction and a *fixed* bootstrapped demonstration set — chosen once, not retrieval-gated, with no per-item notion of coverage — and GEPA evolves instruction text with the memory slot untouched. Reviewers were right that MIPROv2 is the most direct existing instantiation of "couple the instruction with a demonstration set," so it is now a first-class arm (E2 vii) rather than an omission.

**(iii) Memory tiering and classical caching.** MemGPT's core/archival paging and A-MEM's consolidation promote frequently-accessed or recent items into an always-resident tier. Behind them sits four decades of cache admission/eviction theory: Belady's optimal replacement (route by *future* access), LFU/LRU/ARC (route by *past* access), and working-set estimation (estimate future access from a representative recent window). A reviewer correctly observed that "estimate future access from deployment-representative data rather than stale logs" is, at the level of slogan, working-set estimation. We concede that and state precisely what does not carry over:
- **The tiers are not equivalent.** In a cache, the fast and slow tier return the same object with different latency; a miss costs time. Here, instruction residency changes the *content and framing* of the prompt (merged, always present, no gating) and a miss costs a wrong answer, not a delay.
- **The competitive tier is always full.** Top-k always injects exactly k items, so admitting one item evicts another on *every* query. Caches have idle capacity and variable occupancy; this is a permanent zero-sum allocation.
- **The optimal move is inverted.** A hit-rate-maximizing cache promotes the broadest item into the fast tier *to serve it*. We claim promotion is valuable because it *vacates a slot in the competitive tier* — a benefit with no analogue in caching, where fast-tier residency does not free slow-tier capacity. This is exactly what the refill / no-refill / padding controls test, and no capacity-driven paging paper runs them.
- **The objective is accuracy, not hit rate,** which makes it non-obvious that coverage should dominate value. The surprising part of our claim is that a *label-free* coverage statistic beats a *label-expensive* utility statistic.

The pilot behind this track showed the harmful bank retrieved *topically correct* items and that injection **volume** was the causal lever — which is what slot competition predicts and relevance-based accounts of memory harm do not.
Abstract: Agent frameworks store distilled experience in one of two places: an always-on block shipped with every prompt (playbook / cheatsheet methods) or a retrieval-gated bank from which a fixed top-k is injected per query (ExpeL-style memory). The two have never been compared at a matched token budget, and the intermediate question — which items should be promoted into the instruction and which should stay retrievable — has been answered in practice only by usage-frequency paging (MemGPT) and, in theory, by classical cache admission policies. We propose an economic account with a prediction that inverts the caching one. Instruction residency costs tokens on every episode but guarantees availability; bank residency costs tokens only when retrieved but competes for a scarce, always-full set of injection slots. This makes **coverage breadth** — the fraction of the *deployment* query distribution for which an item enters top-k — the deciding statistic, because a broad item occupies a slot on nearly every episode and starves narrow items. Unlike a cache, which promotes broad items to serve them faster, we predict the benefit of promotion is the *vacated slot*. Breadth is computable from unlabeled calibration queries; utility requires labeled probes; usage frequency is measured on past traffic and misleads whenever past traffic is skewed. We test this on multi-hop QA with a local search index and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: an item-level placement regression with breadth, utility and usage entered as competing predictors; a matched-token comparison of no-memory, pure top-k, similarity-threshold retrieval, pure playbook, MemGPT-style usage promotion, MIPROv2 joint instruction+demonstrations, and breadth routing; slot-freeing controls (refill / no-refill / padding) at k=2 where slots are scarcest; oracle-breadth and oracle-placement ceilings that bound the headroom the free statistic leaves on the table; a second dataset (MuSiQue) for the primary contrast; and a threshold-retrieval replication that tests whether the mechanism is specific to fixed-k. Everything is item-paired with McNemar contrasts against a measured null-replicate floor. Total program: 28,300 episodes, ~35 wall-clock hours on one 4×A100 node and under $100 of API.
Experiments:
**Setup.** Task: multi-hop QA. Primary dataset HotpotQA full-wiki; second dataset MuSiQue-Ans (fallback 2WikiMultihopQA if the 7B ReAct agent's base EM on MuSiQue is <15%). Retrieval tool is a **local BM25+dense Wikipedia index** — free, deterministic, cacheable, no API cost and no tool-side noise. Scoring is **exact match** (secondary F1); **no LLM judge**. Agent: ReAct, ~4 LLM calls/episode. Model: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, greedy, fixed seeds. Memory bank: ExpeL/ReasoningBank-style, ~300 items (distilled insights plus successful/failed trajectory summaries) built by a frontier model from 500 history episodes; dense retrieval (bge-large), top-k injection.

**Splits (all disjoint).** *History stream*: 500 episodes with a deliberate **Zipfian topic skew**, used for bank construction and usage counts. *Calibration set*: 500 **unlabeled** queries from the deployment distribution, used only to compute breadth and cutoffs. *Validation*: 300 labeled, for k, similarity cutoff, breadth cutoff. *Held-out*: 800 labeled, paired across all conditions.

**The three routing statistics, separated by construction.**
- **Breadth** b(m) = fraction of the 500 unlabeled calibration queries for which m enters top-k. Zero labels, zero LLM calls.
- **Usage frequency** f(m) = recency-weighted retrieval count over the skewed history stream (the MemGPT/A-MEM/LFU signal). The skew is what makes f and b diverge: a narrow item serving a common past topic gets high f, low b; a general-strategy item distilled from a rare topic gets low f, high b.
- **Utility** u(m) = paired outcome change from single-item injection, estimated with 6 probes each on the 60 highest-retrieval-mass items (360 episodes).

**E0 (Gate and decorrelation check).** (a) Does the bank matter at all: top-k vs no-memory on held-out, in either direction, beyond the measured noise floor. (b) Report Spearman ρ(b,f), ρ(b,u), and the Lorenz curve of retrieval mass. Pre-registered rule: if ρ(b,f) > 0.7, the breadth-vs-frequency arm is declared uninformative *in this setup* and reported as such — no post hoc manufacture of separation; same rule for ρ(b,u). If (a) fails, the paper becomes the matched-token comparison plus a bounded null, stated up front. Cost: validation sweeps for k / similarity cutoff / breadth cutoff (300 × ~7 configs = 2,100) + 360 utility probes + 40 slack = **2,500**.

**E1 (Item-level placement law — the core test).** 14 items spanning the breadth range. For each: (a) item in the instruction, removed from the bank; (b) item in the bank only. Each scored on the same 150 held-out queries, **stratified 75 where m ∈ top-k and 75 where m ∉ top-k**, shared seeds. Four items also get (c) absent entirely. Placement advantage A(m) = acc(instr) − acc(bank), regressed on b(m) in a mixed-effects logistic model with item and query random intercepts and fixed effects for b, u, f and item length. **The tested quantity is the breadth coefficient**, not any single item. A(m) for these 14 items is also the ground truth for the oracle ceiling in E6. Episodes: 14×2×150 + 4×150 = **4,800**.

**E2 (Matched-token system comparison, n=800 paired, k* tuned on validation).** Seven arms, matched on logged mean realized prompt tokens within 5%: (i) no memory; (ii) pure top-k retrieval; (iii) **similarity-threshold retrieval** (variable count above a calibrated cutoff) — the arm that could dissolve the slot-scarcity premise; (iv) pure playbook (highest-utility items merged into an always-on block to budget, no retrieval); (v) **usage-frequency promotion, MemGPT-style** (promote by recency-weighted f, evict on capacity, remainder retrievable); (vi) **breadth-routed hybrid** (consolidate items above the validation-calibrated breadth cutoff into a merged block, remainder retrievable at fixed k, freed slots refilled); (vii) **MIPROv2-style joint optimization** — instruction plus a fixed bootstrapped demonstration set, no retrieval gating, optimization capped at 400 rollouts. Arm (vii) replaces the GEPA-no-memory arm from the previous version, per review: it is the closest existing instantiation of instruction+demonstration coupling and the honest test of whether fixed jointly-optimized demos already buy what breadth routing buys. Episodes: 7×800 + 400 optimization = **6,000**.

**E3 (Slot-freeing controls, at k=2 where slots are scarcest and the predicted effect largest).** (a) breadth hybrid with refill, n=800; (b) same, no refill (freed slots left empty, effective k drops), n=800; (c) drop-only (broad items deleted, no consolidation, refill), n=600; (d) padding (broad items consolidated, freed slots filled with length-matched neutral text), n=600; (e) pure retrieval k=2, n=600. Running at k=2 rather than k=4 is a pre-registered power decision. Episodes: **3,400**.

**E4 (Routing-variable ablation, matched consolidated-token budget, all with refill).** Utility-routed (n=800) and random-routed (n=800) versus breadth (reuse E2 vi) and skewed-frequency (reuse E2 v). Plus **frequency routing computed on an unskewed history stream** (n=400), predicted to converge on breadth routing — the positive control showing the breadth/frequency distinction is about distribution shift, not naming. Episodes: **2,000**.

**E5 (Attribution, free from logs).** For every held-out item the breadth hybrid fixes relative to pure retrieval, record whether its top-k retrieved set changed.

**E6 (Headroom / oracle ceilings) — added per review.** (a) **Oracle-breadth**: breadth recomputed on the 800 held-out queries themselves rather than the calibration sample; the gap to E2 (vi) is pure calibration sampling error. (b) **Oracle-placement**: for the 14 E1 items, place each on the side that E1's held-out-measured A(m) says is better, all other items routed by breadth; the gap to E2 (vi) restricted to those items bounds how much of the achievable placement gain the free statistic captures. n=800 each. Episodes: **1,600**.

**E7 (Second-dataset replication of the primary contrast) — added per review.** MuSiQue-Ans: fresh bank (300 episodes of construction, same skewed-history protocol), 200 unlabeled calibration queries, then four arms at n=600 paired — pure top-k, pure playbook, usage-frequency promotion, breadth hybrid. This tests P2 and the frequency half of P4 on a genuinely different compositional-question distribution. It is a *dataset-level* replication, not a task-family generalization, and is labeled as such. Episodes: 300 + 200 + 4×600 = **2,900**.

**E8 (Retrieval-architecture replication) — added per review.** Breadth hybrid layered on **similarity-threshold retrieval** instead of fixed-k, n=600, compared to the threshold baseline from E2 (iii). Prediction: the hybrid's margin is *smaller* here than under fixed-k, because variable-count admission does not force broad items to evict narrow ones. This converts the reviewer's "the mechanism may be a fixed-k artifact" objection into a signed prediction. Episodes: **600**.

**Noise and variance budget.** Null replicate: rerun pure retrieval k* in full with fresh seeds and score it against itself (800). Three decoding seeds on two key cells at n=400 (1,600). Playbook merge is stochastic: two extra merges for the hybrid and for pure playbook at n=400 (1,600). Total **4,000**.

**Compute arithmetic.** 500 (HotpotQA bank) + 2,500 (E0) + 4,800 (E1) + 6,000 (E2) + 3,400 (E3) + 2,000 (E4) + 1,600 (E6) + 2,900 (E7) + 600 (E8) + 4,000 (noise) = **28,300 episodes**. At ~4 LLM calls/episode ≈ 113k calls, ~1.5k prompt and ~250 output tokens each ⇒ ~170M prefill, ~28M decode. On the 4×A100 node running four vLLM replicas of a 7B model at high concurrency against a free local index, pilot throughput ~800 episodes/hour end-to-end gives **~35 wall-clock hours (~140 GPU-hours)**; we budget 4 days for reruns and orchestration. Frontier-API use is confined to bank distillation (~800 calls across two datasets), playbook merges (~40) and MIPROv2 instruction proposal (~50) — **under $100**.

**Cut and not deferred:** ALFWorld/WebShop, the 3-model grid, the bank-size sweep, the homogeneous-bank replication, the k=8 probe, the GEPA-no-memory arm, and the 14B secondary check. Each was removed because it did not decide a claim, and the freed episodes were spent on the three reviewer-named additions (MIPROv2 arm, oracle ceilings, second dataset) plus the threshold-architecture replication.
Baselines and Ablations:
Baselines that could plausibly win, all at matched realized token budget on the same paired held-out items:
1. **Pure top-k retrieval**, k tuned on validation — the standard agent-memory configuration.
2. **Similarity-threshold (variable-count) retrieval** — if it matches the hybrid at matched tokens, the fixed-k slot-scarcity framing is mechanism-specific, and we report that as the paper's corrected conclusion. E8 makes this a graded rather than binary test.
3. **Usage-frequency promotion, MemGPT/A-MEM/LFU style** — the closest deployed policy. If it matches breadth routing under skewed history, the contribution reduces to a measured explanation of why an existing heuristic works, plus the slot-competition mechanism.
4. **Pure playbook** (Dynamic-Cheatsheet / ACE style always-on block) at the same budget.
5. **MIPROv2-style joint instruction + fixed bootstrapped demonstrations** (added per review) — tests whether jointly-optimized static demos already capture what breadth routing buys.
6. **Drop-only** — the cheapest possible fix. If deleting broad items matches consolidating them, the consolidation machinery is unnecessary.
7. **No memory** and **k=2 unscreened retrieval** (the volume-reduction neutralizer from the pilot).
8. **Oracle-breadth** and **oracle-placement** ceilings (added per review) — bound the headroom left by the free statistic, so a 3-point win over MemGPT can be read as near-optimal or as leaving most of the gain unclaimed.

Ablations isolating the mechanism: (a) refill vs no-refill vs padding-filled freed slots at k=2 — separates slot-freeing from token savings and from duplicate removal; (b) breadth vs utility vs usage-frequency vs random routing at matched consolidated tokens; (c) frequency routing on an unskewed history stream, predicted to converge on breadth — the control proving breadth and frequency are different variables rather than two names for one; (d) LLM-merged playbook vs verbatim concatenation of the same items; (e) instruction length matched by appending neutral text to pure retrieval; (f) cost accounting for the routing statistic itself — breadth needs 0 labeled episodes, utility needed 360.
Falsifiable Predictions:
Minimum detectable effect: n=800 paired at ~12% discordance ⇒ ≈2.5 EM points; n=600 ⇒ ≈2.9. Thresholds are set above these and anything smaller is pre-committed to "indistinguishable," not "trend."

**P1 (placement law).** In E1 the breadth coefficient in the mixed-effects placement regression is positive with a 95% CI excluding zero, after conditioning on utility, usage frequency and item length. Refutation: flat or negative slope — placement does not depend on breadth, which kills the theory.

**P2 (routing beats both endpoints).** At matched tokens the breadth-routed hybrid beats pure top-k retrieval by ≥3 EM points and pure playbook by ≥3 points on HotpotQA (n=800), and beats pure top-k by ≥3.5 points on MuSiQue (n=600). Refutation: within 2.5 points of the better endpoint on the primary dataset — the honest result is then "placement does not matter once tokens are matched," and the matched-token comparison (including the threshold, MemGPT and MIPROv2 arms nobody has run head-to-head) is the contribution.

**P3 (slot-freeing is the mechanism).** At k=2, hybrid-with-refill beats hybrid-without-refill by ≥3 points and beats the padding control by ≥3.5 points (n=600 for padding). Powered only if the total hybrid gain at k=2 is ≥4 points; if smaller we declare the mechanism contrast underpowered rather than reporting a null as evidence. Refutation: no-refill matches refill — the benefit is token savings or duplicate removal, not slot competition.

**P4 (coverage, not utility, not usage).** Breadth routing beats utility routing by ≥3 points at equal consolidated tokens; beats MemGPT-style usage-frequency routing by ≥3 points on HotpotQA and ≥3.5 on MuSiQue under skewed history; and frequency routing on the **unskewed** stream lands within 2.5 points of breadth routing (positive control). Utility and frequency are not significant predictors of placement advantage after conditioning on breadth (E1). Refutation: utility or usage matches breadth under skew, or the unskewed control fails to converge.

**P5 (attribution).** ≥70% of the hybrid's fixes relative to pure retrieval occur on held-out items whose top-k retrieved set changed. Refutation: fixes spread uniformly, implying the consolidated text itself does the work.

**P6 (headroom).** Oracle-breadth is within 2.5 points of calibration-breadth (the free statistic is not sampling-limited), and calibration-breadth recovers ≥50% of the oracle-placement gain restricted to the 14 E1 items. A large oracle-placement gap does not refute the theory but bounds the practical claim, and we report it as such.

**P7 (mechanism is slot-count-dependent, not universal).** The hybrid's margin over its own retrieval baseline is larger under fixed-k (E2) than under similarity-threshold retrieval (E8), by ≥3 points in the difference-of-differences at the pooled n. If threshold retrieval fully matches the fixed-k hybrid at matched tokens, the general "economic law of placement" framing is refuted and the corrected headline is that slot competition is an artifact of fixed-k admission — which is itself a finding worth reporting, since fixed-k is what every deployed agent-memory system uses.
Measurement and Noise Control:
All conditions are scored on identical held-out items with identical decoding seeds; the unit of analysis is the per-item outcome change. Pairwise contrasts use McNemar's exact test on discordant pairs, with **fixes and breaks reported separately**, because the pilot showed net deltas can be flat while composition shifts. Scoring is exact match against gold answers — no LLM judge, so judging noise is eliminated by construction.

Pre-registered primary contrasts, reported uncorrected: (1) breadth hybrid vs pure top-k retrieval (HotpotQA), (2) breadth hybrid vs pure playbook, (3) breadth routing vs usage-frequency routing under skewed history, (4) the breadth coefficient in the E1 placement regression, (5) the same-direction replication of (1) and (3) on MuSiQue. Every other cellwise contrast is Holm-corrected within its experiment. Token matching is enforced on logged realized prompt tokens (means within 5%), and each headline number is additionally shown on an accuracy-versus-tokens curve with item-level bootstrap CIs, so no single matched point carries the argument.

Noise floor: the pure-retrieval cell is rerun in full (n=800) as a **null replicate** — relabelled as a treatment and compared against itself — and two key cells are re-scored under three fresh seeds at n=400. Nothing is claimed unless it exceeds the 95th percentile of that null distribution. The playbook merge is stochastic, so merged blocks are regenerated with three seeds for the hybrid and pure playbook; a difference must exceed twice the across-merge SD.

Power: n=800 paired at ~12% discordance gives ~80% power at ≈2.5 EM points (n=600 ⇒ ≈2.9), which is why P2–P4 are stated at ≥3 / ≥3.5. E1 uses n=150 per item (per-item MDE ~7 points), so no per-item claim is made; the hierarchical model borrows strength across 14 items and the slope is the tested quantity. E8's difference-of-differences is the least-powered primary test and is reported with its CI; if the CI spans zero we report the fixed-k-specificity question as open rather than resolved. Retrieval k, similarity cutoff and breadth cutoff are calibrated on the disjoint validation split; breadth is computed only on the unlabeled calibration split; held-out data is never used for tuning except in the two explicitly-labeled oracle arms, which are reported as ceilings and never as methods.
Preprint Collision Check:
**The literature search run for this proposal returned zero results.** The web search tool failed on every invocation with a server-side "tool use limit exceeded" error, including on a minimal test query, across multiple retries. No titles, dates, venues or abstracts were retrieved. I state plainly: **novelty has not been verified, only asserted.** Silence from a broken tool is not evidence of novelty, and this proposal should be read as having an open, unresolved collision risk. Two rounds of review have flagged this; I cannot fix it with prose and will not pretend otherwise.

**Closest work, from recollection only, explicitly unverified:** MemGPT (core/archival paging with usage- and recency-triggered promotion into an always-resident tier), A-MEM (consolidation under capacity pressure), Dynamic Cheatsheet (Suzgun et al., 2025) and agentic-context-engineering playbooks, ExpeL (AAAI 2024), Agent Workflow Memory (ICML 2025), ReasoningBank-style 2025/26 banks, MIPROv2 (EMNLP 2024) and GEPA. Beyond the LLM literature, the closest *conceptual* prior work — named by a reviewer and now conceded in Related Work — is classical cache admission and replacement: Belady's optimal algorithm, LFU/LRU/ARC, and working-set estimation, which already formalize "route residency by predicted future access, not stale historical frequency."

**Assessment of collision.** On the *decision problem* (where should an item live), MemGPT-style usage promotion collides directly, and we now run it as a first-class baseline (E2 v, E4) rather than a foil. On the *statistic* (deployment-distribution coverage rather than historical frequency), working-set estimation collides at the level of principle; we do not claim that principle as new. What we claim is not covered by either: (a) the tiers are not latency-equivalent — promotion changes prompt content and a miss costs an answer, not a delay; (b) the competitive tier is always exactly full, so admission is eviction on every query; (c) **the optimal move is inverted relative to caching** — a hit-rate-maximizing cache promotes broad items to serve them, whereas we predict the payoff is the vacated slot, which is precisely what the refill / no-refill / padding controls at k=2 test and what no caching or paging paper has reason to run; (d) coverage dominating *utility* is not a caching prediction at all, since caches optimize hit rate rather than downstream value.

**Unresolved risk.** A mid-2025-to-present preprint in the context-engineering / memory-tiering line proposing hot-cold promotion of frequently retrieved memory items into a static prompt, or token-budget-aware allocation between instruction and retrieval, is a natural next step in the ACE/ReasoningBank lineage and I cannot rule it out.

**Commitment.** Before any submission we will run and publish a dated search log — arXiv cs.CL/cs.AI, Semantic Scholar, and citation-forward from MemGPT, ACE/Dynamic Cheatsheet, ReasoningBank and MIPROv2 — over: "memory promotion always-on context agent"; "hot cold memory tiering LLM agent"; "instruction vs retrieval placement distilled experience"; "injection budget allocation agent memory"; "context budget routing playbook retrieval"; "coverage-based memory consolidation agent". If a collision is found, the surviving contribution is the part such a preprint is unlikely to have: the item-level placement regression with breadth, utility and usage entered as competing predictors; the refill/no-refill/padding controls identifying slot competition; the oracle-placement ceiling; and the threshold-retrieval difference-of-differences bounding the mechanism to fixed-k admission. **If a collision is found that also runs those controls, we withdraw the claim rather than reframe it.**
Risk Factors and Limitations:
1. **Unverified novelty.** The search tool failed; the closest-work list is recollection. This is the largest single risk to the proposal and is stated in the Preprint Collision Check rather than softened.
2. **Gate risk.** The study is conditional on the bank mattering at all (E0). If top-k memory is indistinguishable from no memory in either direction, there is no placement question and we report the matched-token comparison as a bounded null with a stated MDE.
3. **Collapsed statistics.** If ρ(b,f) > 0.7 despite the deliberately skewed history stream, P4's frequency arm is uninformative and we say so rather than reinterpreting. Same rule for breadth vs utility. The pre-registered fallback (transparently augmenting the bank with synthetic high-utility narrow and low-utility broad items to decorrelate) is labeled secondary and would support a mechanism claim, not a deployment claim.
4. **Novelty risk against MemGPT and against caching theory.** If usage-frequency promotion matches breadth routing, the contribution reduces to a measured explanation of an existing heuristic plus the slot-competition mechanism. We keep the hypothesis and accept the reduced claim; we refuse to rescue it by broadening the paper into a generic memory survey.
5. **Threshold retrieval could dissolve the premise.** E8 tests this directly. If variable-cutoff retrieval matches the hybrid at matched tokens, the slot-scarcity framing is specific to fixed-k admission and that becomes the headline correction. Note that fixed-k is what deployed systems actually use, so this outcome is informative rather than vacuous — but it is a genuine refutation of the general framing.
6. **One task family.** HotpotQA plus MuSiQue is a dataset-level replication, not cross-family generality; web/tool and code agents are untested. We will not claim generality across task families, and this limitation appears in the abstract. Adding a second family did not fit the envelope; we chose a second dataset and a second retrieval architecture instead, on the grounds that the mechanism claim is about retrieval geometry rather than task semantics.
7. **One model.** Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct only; the 14B check was cut to fund the reviewer-named additions. Scaling behaviour of slot competition is unknown.
8. **Underpowered mechanism contrasts.** P3 needs a ≥4-point total effect at k=2 to separate refill from no-refill; P7's difference-of-differences is the least-powered primary test. If either is small we report the question as open, not settled.
9. **Attention dilution.** Long always-on playbooks may dilute attention independently of placement; the neutral-text length control bounds but does not eliminate this.
10. **Oracle arms touch held-out labels.** E6 is explicitly a ceiling, never a proposed method, and is excluded from all matched-token headline comparisons except as an upper bound.

Name: clause_level_portability
Title: Prompt Optimizers Discover Two Kinds of Text: A Clause-Level Attribution Study of What Transfers Across Domains
Short Hypothesis: The gain produced by a reflective prompt optimizer decomposes at the level of individual clauses into a task-specific part (content, exemplars, domain vocabulary) whose value is confined to the source task, and a domain-general part (output contracts, error-avoidance/edge-case clauses, procedural decomposition) whose value transfers. We predict that a clause's contribution on its source task is a poor predictor of its cross-task contribution, while a cheap clause *type* label is a good one, and that a zero-rollout library of high-portability clauses recovers a substantial, measurable fraction of cold-start GEPA's small-budget gain on held-out domains.
Related Work: (All citations unverified; literature search backend was unavailable.) GEPA (Agrawal et al., 2025), MIPROv2 (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024), OPRO (Yang et al., 2023) and APE (Zhou et al., 2022) return a single monolithic prompt string per task and report only whole-prompt scores; none attributes the gain to parts of the returned prompt, and none measures whether those parts are portable. OPRO's 'Take a deep breath' anecdote and follow-up work on prompt sensitivity/irrelevant-token effects hint that some discovered text is content-free, but this is anecdotal rather than a causal decomposition. SPoT/ATTEMPT (Vu et al., 2021; Asai et al., 2022) transfer soft prompts as indivisible model-bound parameter blocks and predict transfer from task embeddings; a soft prompt has no clause structure to attribute, so the question we ask cannot be posed there. Instruction-induction and prompt-component 'best practice' papers hand-write component taxonomies and test them a priori; we instead *harvest* components from what an optimizer actually discovered and measure their portability causally. Work on cross-model prompt transfer varies the model with the task fixed — the orthogonal axis. The new object here is a clause×target portability matrix estimated by causal insertion/deletion, and the resulting claim that the transferable component of prompt optimization is a small, reusable, model-portable text library rather than a whole prompt or a search procedure.
Abstract: Reflective prompt optimizers return one prompt per task, and every deployment to a new domain pays the full rollout bill again. We ask a more basic question than 'does the prompt transfer?': which *parts* of it do. We optimize eight tasks spanning multi-hop QA, symbolic reasoning, code and instruction following with a reimplemented GEPA, then segment each returned prompt into atomic clauses and label each with a seven-way type taxonomy (role framing, output contract, task-specific content, procedural decomposition, error-avoidance/edge case, exemplar, motivational filler). We estimate two quantities per clause: its causal contribution on its own task, via leave-one-clause-out and random-subset regression, and its causal contribution when inserted into the baseline prompt of each of the seven other tasks. This yields a clause×target portability matrix. Our central hypothesis is a dissociation: source contribution and cross-task contribution are weakly correlated, because the largest source contributions come from task-specific content clauses whose transfer is null or negative, while smaller but reliably positive transfer comes from output-contract and error-avoidance clauses. We then close the loop with a zero-rollout baseline: assemble the top-ranked portable clauses into a generic prefix, apply it to held-out tasks with no target optimization at all, and report the number of cold-start GEPA rollouts it is worth, with a bootstrap interval. Because most measurements are scoring passes rather than optimization runs, the study is affordable on one node, and all claims are referenced against a measured re-scoring noise floor and a treatment-free null replicate.
Experiments:
(1) Noise floor. Re-score 20 fixed prompts on each task's held-out set 5 times; estimate per-task metric SD under decode nondeterminism and sampling of the eval set. Run two cold-start GEPA runs per task differing only in seed to bound the apparent 'gain' obtainable from nothing. Every later threshold references this floor.
(2) Source optimization. Reimplement GEPA (executor: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct locally, replicated on Qwen2.5-32B at reduced scale; reflector: frontier API model). Optimize 8 tasks (2 BBH clusters, 2 Super-NaturalInstructions clusters, HotpotQA, GSM8K, MBPP, an instruction-following set), 300 rollouts × 3 seeds. Keep the validation-argmax prompt per seed.
(3) Clause segmentation and typing. An LLM splits each final prompt into atomic clauses (target 6–18 per prompt; sentence/bullet granularity, deterministic post-check that concatenation reproduces the original). Two independent LLM judges plus a human spot-check assign each clause one of 7 types; report inter-judge agreement (Cohen's kappa) on all clauses and human agreement on a 100-clause sample. Expect ~100–300 clauses total per seed pool.
(4) Within-source attribution. Per task: (a) leave-one-clause-out, scoring the ablated prompt on a 200-example held-out set; (b) random-subset estimation — sample 80 random clause subsets, score each, and regress score on clause-presence indicators to get shapley-style marginals with standard errors. Total ~8 tasks × ~100 evaluations × 200 examples ≈ 160k generations, batched with vLLM.
(5) Cross-task portability. For each of the 8 targets, take each clause from the other 7 tasks' prompts, insert it into the target's fixed baseline prompt (position controlled: appended in a fixed slot), and score on the target's held-out set. This is the clause×target matrix. To control cost, first pool clauses by near-duplicate merging and cap at ~120 unique clauses; 120 × 7 targets × 200 examples ≈ 168k generations. Also score a length-matched filler control clause and a semantically-inverted variant of each clause (a 'sham clause' saying the opposite) to distinguish content from mere token addition.
(6) The dissociation test.
