All three are identity/style accounts, which are symmetric: they predict that 8B-written memory hurts a 14B reader as much as the reverse. We predict asymmetry, and the asymmetry is the discriminating test. None reports a fix/break decomposition, a quality/utility rank inversion, or the selection-vs-authorship contrast; all three propose *content-side* engineering (adapters, contrastive disentanglement, hierarchical structure) rather than asking whether on-policy *selection* alone suffices.

**(2) Harm-mechanism accounts we adjudicate against.** *When Continual Learning Moves to Memory* (2604.27003) and *Cross-Component Interference in LLM Agent Scaffolding* (2605.05716) give volume/interference accounts; *MemHarness* (2607.28272) and *Experience-Following Behavior* (2505.16067) give content/error-propagation accounts; *Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated* (2605.12978) gives a same-model consolidation-drift account. In every one of them the distiller is a frontier model and the agent is not, and that asymmetry is never a variable. Our matched-intersection design holds volume, item count, task coverage and trajectory success fixed so these accounts cannot produce our predicted effect.

**(3) Distillation with student-aware supervision.** *Distilling LLM Agent into Small Models* (NeurIPS 2025, 2505.17612), SCoRe (2509.14257) and Personalised Distillation (2310.18628) establish that teacher supervision must match student competence — but in the weight-update regime. Whether the mismatch survives into the training-free, inference-time regime, where the reader merely has to *follow* text rather than fit it, is not entailed and is what we measure.

**(4) Prompt optimization.** GEPA/MIPRO evolve instructions by scoring candidates on the deploying model's own rollouts. The literature reads this as search efficiency. We read it as an on-policy admission test on the instruction slot, and use it as the mechanism-isolating comparison for the memory slot: same frontier author, differing only in whether the reader selected.

Our contribution: turn "cross-model memory is hard" into a signed, measurable law with a predicted rank inversion; separate authorship from selection as the operative variable; and show that coupling memory to a prompt optimizer masks provenance harm end-to-end, which is a direct answer to the track's co-adaptation and measurement questions.
Abstract:
Agentic memory pipelines almost universally have a frontier model distill experience that a small agent then consumes. The field treats this provenance asymmetry as an implementation detail; recent cross-model memory work (Rosetta Memory, MemCollab, AMD) has noticed that it matters but frames it as model-identity mismatch to be patched. We argue it is a signed, ordinal effect: memory is advice, advice is only useful to a policy that can execute it, so utility falls with the *directed* writer→reader capability gap and downward transfer is harmful in a way upward transfer is not. We further argue the cure is not reader authorship but reader-in-the-loop selection — and that this is exactly what a GEPA-style prompt optimizer already does to the instruction slot, which is why coupling an optimizer to a memory bank produces end-to-end gains that cannot be attributed to either part.

We test this in one environment (tool-augmented multi-hop QA) with a transplant matrix that holds source tasks constant: two self-hosted readers (8B, 14B) plus a frontier writer distill memory from the *intersection* of training instances all agents solved, so every bank covers the same tasks, all from successful trajectories, at matched item count and matched injected tokens; only the writing policy varies. Both transfer directions are run, which separates our signed-gap account from the symmetric identity-mismatch account of prior work. A blind pairwise quality judging pass tests the predicted rank inversion. Two selection arms — reader-probe admission on the frontier memory bank, and GEPA (frontier-authored instructions, reader-selected) versus frontier-authored-but-unselected instructions — isolate selection from authorship in both slots. A faithful, uncontrolled teacher→student replication confirms the literature's positive effect reproduces here before we attribute its disappearance to our controls. 33 evaluation runs, ~21k episodes total, fits one 4×A100 node in days.
Experiments:
**HELD FIXED.** ReAct scaffold, retriever and similarity function, deployment top-k, decoding temperature and seed schedule, tool stack, step limit, prompt boilerplate, and the set of training instances from which memory derives. Free variables: writer identity, reader identity, instruction condition, and whether the reader selected.

**ENVIRONMENT (one only).** Tool-augmented multi-hop QA: HotpotQA-distractor + MuSiQue, agent issues search calls, 4–8 model calls per episode. 500 train instances (bank construction + GEPA), 150 dev (precheck), 500 held-out test, disjoint. *We do not claim generality beyond tool-augmented QA and say so in the paper.*

**POLICIES.** Readers: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. Writers: those two, plus a frontier API model (writer/reflector/judge only). Cross-family equal-capability pair: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.

**BANK CONSTRUCTION — THE IDENTIFICATION STEP.** Run both self-hosted agents on the 500 train instances. Take the intersection of instances both solved (expect 150–250). For each writer, distill one item per intersection instance from *that writer's own* successful trajectory using an identical distillation prompt. Result: one bank per writer over identical tasks, identical item count, all from successes. The frontier writer has no trajectories of its own, so it distills from the 14B agent's traces on the same instances (this is the strongest realistic version of current practice); one extra bank has the frontier writer distill from the *8B's own* traces, decomposing "who acted" from "who wrote." Items truncated/padded to equalize per-bank median token length within 5%; injected token count per episode matched across banks. Two independent bank replicates per writer from disjoint halves of the intersection.

**PRECHECK (dev, 150 instances).** At least one bank must move ≥4% of instances wrong→right versus no memory for at least one reader. Reported regardless of outcome; an inert bank makes the transplant comparison vacuous.

**RUN LIST (each 500 test instances, fully paired, unless noted).**
- A. Base instructions, no memory, 8B / 14B — 2 runs.
- B. Base + self-written bank, 8B / 14B × 2 bank replicates — 4 runs.
- C. Base + frontier bank (from 14B traces), 8B / 14B × 2 replicates — 4 runs.
- D. Base + other self-hosted writer's bank: 8B reads 14B-written; 14B reads 8B-written — 2 runs. **(the direction-asymmetry cells)**
- E. Base + frontier bank distilled from the 8B's *own* traces, 8B reader — 1 run. (who-acted vs who-wrote)
- F. **AMD-faithful uncontrolled arm** (reviewer-requested): frontier-written bank over the *full* train split, unmatched task coverage, retrieval as published, 8B / 14B — 2 runs.
- G. GEPA instructions (frontier reflector proposes, candidates scored on the reader's own train rollouts), no memory, 8B / 14B — 2 runs.
- H. GEPA instructions + self bank — 2 runs.
- I. GEPA instructions + frontier bank — 2 runs.
- J. **Frontier-authored instructions, no reader selection** (frontier writes its best instruction cold), no memory, 8B / 14B — 2 runs. (isolates selection from authorship in the instruction slot; same author as G)
- K. Base + **reader-probe-selected** frontier bank: keep only frontier items that survive 3 probe replays by the reader; token-matched by padding to the same injected budget — 2 runs. (isolates selection from authorship in the memory slot)
- L. Cross-family control, n=300: Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B each read own and each other's bank (banks built over their own solved intersection) — 4 runs.
- M. Null replicates: four designated cells (A-8B, B-8B, C-8B, I-8B) re-run at a second decoding seed — 4 runs.

**33 runs; 29×500 + 4×300 = 15,700 evaluation episodes.** Plus bank-construction rollouts (3 agents × 500 = 1,500), GEPA optimization (6 reader×bank conditions × 12 candidates × 40 minibatch episodes = 2,880), probe replay (150 items × 3 probes × 2 readers = 900). **Total ≈ 21,000 episodes ≈ 125k model calls**, ~85% on 8B/14B under vLLM tensor-parallel on 4×A100. At a conservative 20 episodes/min aggregate this is ~18 GPU-hours for the 8B share and ~2× that for the 14B share: **2–3 days wall clock.** API spend: frontier distillation (~450 items × ~2k tok) ≈ $10; GEPA reflection (6 runs × 12 proposals) ≈ $20; blind pairwise judging (500 pairs) ≈ $25; executability annotation (400 items) ≈ $15. **Total under $100**, leaving headroom for one re-run.

**ANALYSIS PASSES (no extra rollouts).**
- *Quality/utility dissociation.* Blind pairwise judging of matched items (same source task, different writer) on generality, correctness, actionability: 250 pairs for 8B-vs-frontier and 250 for 14B-vs-frontier. 100-pair author-rated subset for judge validation (Cohen's κ).
- *Executability readout.* LLM annotator extracts the concrete actions/tool calls each injected item recommends (validated on 100 human-checked cases); measure fraction the reader attempts and fraction it attempts-but-malforms, from logs already collected in runs B and C.
- *Abstraction as rival mechanism.* Judge-scored specificity per item (same judging pass) tested as a mediator: if strong writers simply write vaguer advice, that is the mechanism and we report it as such.
- *Shuffled-provenance placebo.* Re-analyze run C logs with items relabelled to the wrong writer; confirms measured differences track item text, not bookkeeping.
Baselines and Ablations:
**Baselines that could win and would refute us.**
(i) *Frontier bank ≥ self bank for both readers under matched controls* — AMD's implicit prediction; the most likely way the hypothesis dies. We would then report that item quality dominates provenance and the field's default pipeline is right.
(ii) *AMD-faithful uncontrolled arm (F)* — the reviewer-named missing baseline. If the published positive effect does **not** reproduce here, a negative controlled result is uninterpretable (bad reimplementation vs real confound) and we say so before drawing any conclusion. This run gates the whole paper's negative-result reading.
(iii) *No memory (A)* — must be beaten by some bank or the study is about nothing.
(iv) *Reader-probe selection (K) fully rescuing the frontier bank* — this does not refute the gap; it refutes the *authorship* reading and changes the recommendation from "write with the consumer" to "select with the consumer." Equally reportable, and it is our own second prediction.
(v) *GEPA alone (G) beating every memory condition* — would show the instruction slot subsumes the demonstration slot in this environment, an answer to the track's division-of-labour question that we would report as such.
(vi) *Symmetric harm in run D* — the identity-mismatch account of Rosetta Memory / MemCollab. If harm is symmetric, our signed-gap framing is wrong and theirs is right.

**Ablations isolating the mechanism.** The intersection-bank construction (same tasks, all successes, matched item count, matched injected tokens) is the core control — writer identity is the only free variable, which rules out volume, coverage and success-rate accounts by construction. Run D provides both transfer directions (signed vs symmetric). Run E separates who acted from who wrote. Run L (cross-family, equal capability) separates capability gap from stylistic self-affinity. Runs J vs G separate selection from authorship holding the author fixed in the instruction slot; run K vs C does the same in the memory slot. Abstraction-mediation tests the "strong writers write vaguer advice" reduction. Shuffled-provenance placebo checks bookkeeping.
Falsifiable Predictions:
All thresholds are set at or above the stated minimum detectable effect for that contrast.

1. **Signed asymmetry (primary).** For the 8B reader, the frontier bank underperforms its self-written bank by ≥4 net accuracy points, paired, McNemar p<0.05, direction replicated in both bank replicates. The mirror comparison — 14B reading the 8B-written bank versus its own — shows no penalty of comparable size, and the difference-in-differences on *break counts* (the more sensitive, one-sided endpoint) is ≥6 points. A symmetric identity-mismatch account predicts equal harm in both directions and is falsified by this cell.
2. **Quality/utility rank inversion.** Frontier items win ≥65% of blind pairwise quality judgments against 8B-written items (judge κ≥0.5 versus human ratings) while losing on downstream utility for the 8B reader. If quality and utility rank together, this claim dies.
3. **Breaks, not missing fixes.** The frontier bank breaks ≥2× as many instances for the 8B reader as the self bank does, at comparable fix counts.
4. **Selection, not authorship (the mechanism claim).** (a) Reader-probe-selected frontier memory (K) recovers ≥50% of the self-vs-frontier gap for the 8B reader at matched injected tokens. (b) In the instruction slot, GEPA (frontier-authored, reader-selected) beats frontier-authored-unselected instructions (J) by ≥4 points for the 8B reader — same author, selection is the only difference. If (a) fails while (b) holds, the two slots behave differently and we report that as the division-of-labour finding.
5. **Masking (the coupling claim).** Under GEPA-evolved instructions, the net accuracy difference between self-written and frontier-written memory (H vs I) falls below the MDE for both readers, *while* the break-count asymmetry from prediction 3 persists at ≥60% of its base-instruction magnitude. That is: end-to-end evaluation of a coupled optimizer+memory system cannot detect provenance harm that is still there. If instead the gap widens under GEPA, the co-adaptation story is amplification rather than masking — also a finding, stated in advance.
6. **Replication gate.** The uncontrolled AMD-faithful arm (F) shows a positive net gain from frontier memory for at least one reader. If it does not, we report a failed replication and do **not** claim our controls flipped the sign.
7. **Executability.** The 8B reader attempts frontier-recommended actions ≥15 points less often, and malforms them ≥2× as often, as actions recommended by its own items.

**Refutation.** If the frontier bank matches or beats the self bank for both readers under the intersection controls, the provenance account is dead and teacher→student memory transfer is vindicated; we report that as the primary result. If run D shows symmetric harm, or run L shows a same-model advantage as large as the cross-capability one, the effect is identity/style mismatch as Rosetta Memory and MemCollab describe it, not a signed capability gap, and we say so — our contribution then reduces to an independent controlled confirmation of their phenomenon plus the selection-vs-authorship result, which stands on its own.
Measurement and Noise Control:
Three variance sources handled separately.

**(a) Evaluation variance.** Every held-out instance is run under every cell with the same seed schedule, so all reader-holding-constant comparisons are within-instance. Primary test: exact McNemar on fix/break counts, Holm-corrected across the bank family within each reader. Every delta is reported with its full fix/break decomposition, because a null net delta hiding symmetric churn is a different finding from an inert bank — and, per prediction 5, that distinction is the point.

**(b) Bank-construction variance.** Two independent bank replicates per writer from disjoint halves of the intersection, on the two primary contrasts (self and frontier banks, both readers). Analysis is a mixed-effects logistic model with crossed random intercepts for test instance and bank replicate; CIs from a cluster bootstrap resampling bank replicates as well as instances. Non-primary cells use one replicate and are reported as directional only.

**(c) Null replicates.** Four designated cells re-run under a different decoding seed (run M). No effect is claimed unless it exceeds the largest apparent delta observed across these treatment-free repeats. This is load-bearing: prior pilot work in this setting saw re-scoring drift of 5–14 points on small held-out sets and a treatment-free replicate that mimicked the best real treatment.

**Minimum detectable effects.** n=500 paired instances, expected 12–18% discordant-pair rate (60–90 discordant pairs) → McNemar detects ~4–5 net points at 80% power, α=0.05, for a single bank pair; pooling two bank replicates under the mixed model brings the primary self-vs-frontier contrast to ~4 points, which is why prediction 1 is stated at 4. Break-count endpoints are more sensitive because the predicted effect is one-sided (~3 points). The direction-asymmetry difference-in-differences (run D) has roughly √2 the variance of a single contrast → MDE ~6 points, which is why prediction 1's DiD threshold is 6 and why we use break counts there. The cross-family control (n=300, one replicate) has MDE ~6–7 points: **it can rule out a large stylistic-affinity effect but not a small one, and we will not read a sub-6-point null there as evidence of parity.** Judge reliability reported as Cohen's κ against 100 author-rated pairs; the quality half of the dissociation is claimed only if κ>0.5.

**Preregistration.** Predictions 1–7, thresholds, the precheck criterion and the analysis model are fixed before any test-split evaluation is run.
Preprint Collision Check:
The search returned three papers that collide, and the collision is real — I state it plainly rather than arguing it away.

**Closest: Rosetta Memory (arXiv:2606.07711, 2026).** It independently arrives at the diagnosis that memory utility depends on the write-model/read-model relationship rather than content alone, and proposes LLM-aware write/read operators. This **collides on the phenomenon and on part of the framing**. It does not collide on the claim: Rosetta's account is identity/style mismatch, which is symmetric in the model pair, and its fix is a content-side adapter. Our claim is that the effect is *signed and ordinal in capability* (run D is the discriminating test that Rosetta does not run), and our proposed cure is on-policy *selection* rather than content adaptation. If run D shows symmetric harm, Rosetta is right and we say so in the paper.

**MemCollab (arXiv:2603.23234, 2026)** shows naive cross-model transfer degrades performance due to model-specific bias entangled in stored memories, and fixes it contrastively. Same disposition as Rosetta: phenomenon overlaps, mechanism claim does not, and it reports no fix/break decomposition and no quality/utility dissociation.

**AMD (arXiv:2608.07169, 2026)** is the empirical competitor in the opposite direction, and the search result is more damaging than my previous read: AMD explicitly reports that generic memory baselines in the teacher→student setting "yield inconsistent improvements and in several cases degrade performance," and that transfer quality "depends on both teacher accuracy and teacher–student compatibility." So **the existence of the harm, and even a compatibility term, is prior work.** What remains ours: making compatibility a *measured, signed* variable at matched task coverage and matched injected tokens; the predicted quality/utility rank inversion; the selection-vs-authorship dissociation; and the masking result under prompt optimization. AMD's uncontrolled pipeline is now an explicit baseline (run F).

Also retrieved and dispositioned: *Distilling LLM Agent into Small Models* (NeurIPS 2025, 2505.17612) — capability-gap intuition in the weight-update regime, not training-free memory; *Experience-Following Behavior* (2505.16067) and *Useful Memories Become Faulty When Continuously Updated* (2605.12978) — error-propagation and self-consolidation-drift accounts of memory harm, both same-model, both controlled out by our matched-intersection construction; *Cross-Component Interference in LLM Agent Scaffolding* (2605.05716) — component-interaction account, relevant to prediction 5 and cited there; *Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents* survey (2603.07670) — positioning only.

**Honest assessment.** The novelty of "cross-model agent memory transfers badly" is gone as of mid-2026. I am not claiming it. The claims I am defending are the signed-asymmetry law, the quality/utility inversion, the selection-not-authorship cure, and the masking of provenance harm by a prompt optimizer; nothing in the retrieved literature tests any of the four. No matching OpenReview submission was found. Residual risk: a self-written-bank ablation may sit in an appendix of a cross-model memory preprint I did not retrieve; if so, our identification (matched intersection, both directions, token-matched) and the masking result remain distinct.
Risk Factors and Limitations:
1. **Single environment.** Tool-augmented multi-hop QA carries all quantitative claims. Memory in QA is thinner in procedural content than in ALFWorld or WebShop, so effects may be conservative; equally, the result may not transfer to long-horizon control. We scope the paper's claim to this setting explicitly rather than gesturing at generality. Dropping ALFWorld/WebShop was necessary to fit the envelope; underpowered nominal replications would have been worse than none.
2. **Only two capability levels self-hosted.** The "gap slope" is estimated from three gap values (0, ±1 step, +2 via frontier), not a smooth ladder. The signed-asymmetry test (run D) does not need a slope, so the primary claim survives; a monotone dose-response claim would not, and we do not make one.
3. **Intersection size and difficulty.** If both agents solve only easy instances, all banks encode trivial experience and effects shrink. We report intersection size and difficulty distribution; the AMD-faithful arm (F) provides the uncontrolled, full-coverage comparison.
4. **The frontier writer has no trajectories of its own** and distills from the 14B's traces — this weakens the extremity of the gap manipulation, though it is exactly what deployed pipelines do. Run E (frontier writing from the 8B's own traces) and the 8B-vs-14B writer contrast provide fully self-consistent backstops.
5. **Cross-family control is coarse.** One pair, n=300, MDE ~6–7 points: it can exclude a large stylistic-affinity explanation, not a small one, and we say so in the results rather than reading its null as parity.
6. **The masking prediction depends on GEPA budget.** With a larger optimization budget the optimizer might absorb more provenance harm, with a smaller one less. We report the budget and treat prediction 5 as conditional on it; a budget sweep is out of envelope.
7. **Judged quality is a proxy** for what the literature means by "good memory." We validate against human ratings, but a reviewer may reasonably argue a better metric would not invert. We discuss this rather than claiming metric-independence.
8. **Negative result risk.** If frontier memory wins everywhere, the value of the paper rests entirely on the controls plus the successful replication in run F — which is why F, the null replicates and the stated MDEs are load-bearing rather than decorative.

Name: query_agnostic_curation_ceiling
Title: Bounded Before the Query: A Measured Ceiling on Query-Agnostic Memory Curation in LLM Agents
Short Hypothesis: The value of a stored memory item to an agent lives almost entirely in the item×query cell, not in the item. This implies a bound that no write-time curation paper has tested: with the bank frozen and injection volume held exactly fixed, the *best achievable query-agnostic policy* — a global-best static configuration fitted leave-one-instance-out, a set-level oracle prune fitted on unlimited probe data, a Memory-R1-style sequential bank editor, or a GEPA reflective search over a static demonstration set — gains ≤2 points over a random equal-volume selection, while a *query-conditional* policy fitted from the identical training data at the identical k gains ≥5, and an outcome-informed conditional oracle ≥8. The strongest form we will defend: a **training-free cross-encoder reranker**, which has no outcome supervision at all, beats the oracle static prune that was handed unlimited outcome supervision. If that holds, the bound is a property of the policy class (decide-before-query) and not of estimator quality, search budget, or training signal — and any published write-time curation gain exceeding the measured static ceiling must come from bank shrinkage / injection-volume reduction rather than selection quality, which we test head-on with a matched-volume random-removal control that appears in none of the curation papers we could find.
Related Work:
**(1) The audited class: query-agnostic write-time curation.** A-MAC, "Adaptive Memory Admission Control for LLM Agents" (arXiv:2603.04549, ICLR 2026), gates admission on a per-item five-factor value score (future utility, factual confidence, semantic novelty, recency, content-type prior). SAGE (arXiv:2605.30711) gates on novelty; A-MemGuard (arXiv:2510.02373) on consensus; Memory-R1 (arXiv:2508.19828) trains an RL manager emitting per-item ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP; "Memory as a Controlled Process" (arXiv:2607.13591) frames retention as a learned control policy. AutoManual (NeurIPS 2024) validates distilled rules before consolidation; EDV (arXiv:2606.24428) verifies distilled experience with a separate agent; TOKI (arXiv:2606.06240) resolves contradictions at write time. Every one commits an item's fate before the query is known. None reports the ceiling of that policy class, and — as far as we can find — none reports a matched-volume random-removal control, so none of their gains is separable from the effect of shipping a smaller bank.

**(2) The read-time family, and the 2026 evidence that it dominates.** This literature has grown fast and it is now the main threat to our novelty, so we state it plainly. "Diagnosing Retrieval vs. Utilization Bottlenecks in LLM Agent Memory" (arXiv:2603.02473, 2026) runs a 3×3 factorial of write strategy (raw chunks / Mem0 fact extraction / MemGPT summarization) × retrieval method (cosine / BM25 / hybrid rerank) on LoCoMo and finds retrieval spans 20 points while write strategy spans only 3–8, with raw chunking matching expensive curation. CMI (arXiv:2605.17641) reselects memories at read time by estimated performance change rather than similarity. MemArbiter (arXiv:2608.02113) arbitrates among banks at decision time. LazyMem (arXiv:2607.22690) defers construction to read time. MemAct (arXiv:2510.12635) RL-optimizes in-episode context edits. A rate–distortion framing (arXiv:2607.08032) argues the bottleneck is read-side. **Directionally, "read beats write" is no longer a surprising claim, and we do not claim it.** What none of these does: hold injection volume fixed (2603.02473's write strategies produce systematically different item lengths, so its central comparison is volume-confounded); measure what the *best possible* query-agnostic policy could achieve rather than comparing three arbitrary ones; decompose the outcome variance into decoding noise, query main effect, configuration main effect, and configuration×query interaction; or run a matched-volume random-removal control. Our disagreement with 2603.02473 is decidable: its account attributes the small write-side span to the three particular write strategies being near-equivalent, which leaves room for a better-chosen or oracle write-side policy to recover much of the headroom; ours says any query-agnostic policy is bounded near random at matched volume no matter how well chosen. C3 (set-level oracle static prune) versus C2 (matched-volume random prune) decides it.

**(3) Per-example attribution.** Datamodels (Ilyas et al., 2022) supply the randomized-subset regression we adapt to injection. DemoShapley (arXiv:2410.07523), influence-based ICL selection (arXiv:2302.11042), InfICL (arXiv:2402.11750) estimate per-demonstration value in static single-turn ICL. "Helpful or Harmful Data?" (arXiv:2406.04606) studies sign robustness of instance scores. All are *estimator-reliability* critiques. Ours is a bound on a policy class measured with an oracle handed the estimation problem for free — a strictly stronger and less familiar statement than "the estimator is noisy."

**(4) Query-conditional demonstration selection in classical ICL.** KATE (Liu et al., 2021) and Rubin et al. (2022) already show per-query nearest-neighbour demonstration retrieval beats a fixed demonstration set. A reviewer is right that the *direction* of our effect is anticipated there. What is not anticipated: the magnitude of the gap when the static side is an oracle rather than a hand-picked fixed set; the demonstration that the gap survives when the conditional side is given *no outcome supervision at all* (C6) while the static side is given unlimited supervision (C3); and the transfer of this to agent memory banks, where the field is currently investing in write-time admission control rather than read-time selection.

**(5) Prompt optimization and evaluation noise.** GEPA and MIPRO treat a prompt as instructions plus demonstrations and search reflectively; a GEPA-style search over the demonstration slot is the strongest available *static* selection policy and enters as a refutation baseline, not a citation. "On Randomness in Agentic Evals" (arXiv:2602.07150) measures 2.2–6.0 point pass@1 variance; arXiv:2512.21326 and arXiv:2503.07329 decompose seed variance. None decomposes the variance of an intervention component's effect.
Abstract: Agent-memory curation — learned admission control, verify-before-write, contradiction pruning, judge filtering — decides an item's fate before the query is known. Recent work has shown directionally that read-time retrieval matters more than write-time strategy; we ask the sharper question of whether the write-time policy class can work *at all*, and answer it with a bound. On tool-augmented multi-hop QA with an open-weight 14B ReAct agent and a frozen 120-item experience bank, we run a dense factorial probe: 200 held-out instances × 8 fixed injection configurations (each exactly 4 items drawn from the retriever's top-12, so volume is identical everywhere) × 6 decoding seeds, split 3 fit / 3 eval. From these episodes we obtain a non-parametric variance decomposition — decoding noise identified by within-cell seed replication, not assumed — and the paper's decisive contrast: three policies fitted from *identical* training data (the other 199 instances) and scored on the same held-out seeds, differing only in hypothesis class. P1 is the best constant configuration (the ceiling on any query-agnostic policy in the pool); P2 is a feature-only conditional policy with no access to the target instance's outcomes; P3 is an outcome-informed conditional oracle. We predict P1−random ≤2, P2−random ≥5, P3−random ≥8. Because P1 is a constant policy, it is evaluated with 1,200 episodes per configuration and its confidence interval is ±2.5 points, so a null there is informative. Held-out policy evaluation on 600 fresh paired instances pits a faithful A-MAC prune, a judge prune, a Memory-R1-style sequential bank editor, a set-level oracle static prune fitted on unlimited probe data, and a GEPA reflective static demonstration search against two conditional policies at matched k — including a *training-free* cross-encoder reranker with no outcome supervision. The boldest claim we take on: that training-free conditional selector beats the oracle static prune. A matched-volume random-removal control, absent from every curation paper we found, separates selection quality from bank shrinkage and determines whether published write-time gains survive. ~26,000 episodes, one node, under $200 API, pre-stated null bands.
Experiments:
**PRIMARY METRIC.** Token-level F1 on the final answer (continuous, lower variance), with exact match and a fix/break decomposition reported alongside as the interpretable secondary. No LLM judge on outcomes — removes a noise source and an API cost. The switch from EM to F1 as primary is a power decision, stated up front: it roughly halves the standard deviation of paired per-instance differences and is what makes the ±3-point null bands in Phase 3 reachable at 600 instances.

**SCOPE.** One environment, one primary model carry every quantitative claim; a reduced dense replication on a second model tests only the *ordering* (static ceiling < conditional gain). ALFWorld, WebShop, and an OOD slice are cut, not deferred: they cost episodes the centerpiece needs, and an underpowered second environment would not have settled generality anyway.

**HELD FIXED.** ReAct scaffold, BGE retriever over the bank, tool stack, 8-call step limit, temperature 0.7 with an explicit seed schedule, prompt boilerplate, the bank (built once, frozen). In the centerpiece, *how many* items are injected is fixed at k=4; only *which* varies.

**ENVIRONMENT.** Tool-augmented multi-hop QA: mixed HotpotQA-distractor + MuSiQue with a Wikipedia search tool.

**MODELS.** Primary Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct on vLLM, TP=2, two replicas across 4×A100. Secondary Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. A frontier API model performs trajectory→item distillation, API-side proxy scoring, GEPA reflection, and the sequential bank-editor policy, identically across conditions.

**PHASE 0 — BANK + PRECHECK (700 episodes).** Run the agent on 400 training instances; distill each episode into an ExpeL-style item (insight + condensed trajectory); dedupe to 120 items. Precheck on 150 dev instances: the standard top-k memory agent must differ from the no-memory agent on ≥8% of instances in either direction. If not, item valuation is vacuous; we report the precheck and stop rather than proceeding silently.

**PHASE 1 — CENTERPIECE: DENSE FACTORIAL CONDITIONAL PROBE (9,600 + 1,200 reference episodes).** 200 probe instances, disjoint from Phase 3. For each instance, retrieve top-12 candidates; define 8 configurations as fixed *rank patterns* of size 4 over ranks 1–12 under a balanced incomplete block design, each rank appearing in 2–3 configurations. Run every instance × configuration × 6 seeds = 48 episodes/instance. Rank patterns make configurations comparable across instances, which is what makes "the best global static policy" well-defined. References: no-memory and standard top-4 on the same 200 instances × 3 seeds.

*Readouts, all from these episodes, no extra rollouts.*

- **R1 Non-parametric variance decomposition.** Within-cell across-seed variance = decoding noise, measured directly. Across-configuration within-instance variance minus the seed component = configuration×query interaction. Across-instance variance of configuration-averaged outcome = query main effect. Across-instance average of configuration contrasts = configuration main effect. Every component identified by replication rather than by a random-effects fit to sparse cells. Bootstrap CIs over instances.
- **R2 Config-sensitivity fraction.** Percentage of instances whose across-configuration outcome spread exceeds the seed-noise 95th percentile — what fraction of episodes have their outcome decided by *which* equally-sized set of topically-retrieved items was injected.
- **R3 THE DECISIVE CONTRAST — four policies, all at k=4, all scored on the same 3 held-out eval seeds per instance.**
  - **P0 Random configuration:** expected value over the 8 configurations.
  - **P1 Best constant configuration:** for each target instance, the configuration with the best mean outcome across the *other 199* instances (leave-one-instance-out, all 6 of their seeds). The ceiling on any query-agnostic policy within the pool. Note the asymmetry that makes this test strong: because P1 is a constant policy, each candidate configuration's mean is estimated from 1,200 episodes, giving a ±2.5-point CI on P1−P0.
  - **P2 Feature-only conditional policy — the headline:** a model predicting outcome from (configuration × query-feature interactions), fitted on the *same* other-199 data as P1, with **no access to the target instance's outcomes**; at test time it picks the argmax configuration for the target query from features alone. Features: query embedding (PCA to 32 dims), question type, hop count, retriever score profile across ranks 1–12, per-rank cross-encoder relevance, item length/type at each selected rank. P1 and P2 are nested: the same estimator with and without query-feature interaction terms. The contrast is therefore a clean hypothesis-class comparison at identical data, identical k, identical retriever, identical bank.
  - **P3 Outcome-informed conditional oracle:** the configuration with the best outcome on that instance's own 3 *fit* seeds, evaluated on its 3 disjoint eval seeds. This uses partial ground-truth outcome signal and is **explicitly not a deployable selector**; it is reported as an upper reference on recoverable conditional value, and P2 — not P3 — carries the claim. (Best-on-eval-seeds is also reported, labelled overfit and load-bearing for nothing.)

**PHASE 2 — SPARSE RANDOMIZED INJECTION FOR ITEM-IDENTITY EFFECTS (2,400 episodes).** Separate probe instances; each episode injects k~U{1..6} items drawn uniformly from the retriever's top-20. Fits a ridge-regularized logistic datamodel of success on item-presence indicators plus an injected-token-count regressor and a query random intercept (~70 appearances/item; items under 40 excluded, coverage reported). Supplies: the set-level oracle static prune (C3), the training signal for the conditional gate (C5), item-level posteriors for the proxy audit, and the fraction of items whose 95% credible interval excludes zero. A matched-pair leave-one-out contrast on episode pairs differing in exactly one item is computed from the same episodes as an estimator-agreement check.

**PHASE 3 — HELD-OUT POLICY EVALUATION (7,800 episodes).** 600 fresh instances, fully instance-paired, one fixed seed schedule, all conditions on all instances.

*Query-agnostic (the bounded class):*
- **C0** Full bank, standard top-4 (deployment default).
- **C1** A-MAC faithful: prune bottom 12 items by a reimplementation of the five-factor admission score.
- **C2** Matched-volume random prune: remove 12 items at random; 2 independent draws, each on all 600 instances; across-draw spread is the reference band.
- **C3** Set-level oracle static prune: greedy backward elimination of 12 items maximizing predicted mean outcome under the full Phase-2 datamodel, i.e. a *set*-level rather than marginal oracle, so that combinatorial redundancy effects are inside the oracle's reach. This is the strongest static item curation we can construct; a null here cannot be blamed on a weak estimator.
- **C4** GEPA-style reflective search over which items occupy the static demonstration slot; 1,200 search episodes, evaluated once. The strongest static *search*.
- **C9** Judge prune: bottom 12 by LLM-judge item quality.
- **C10** Sequential LLM bank editor: a Memory-R1-style prompted ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP policy streamed over the 400 training episodes, producing a curated bank. Query-agnostic by construction, and it covers the sequential/history-dependent write policy that a single-shot admission oracle does not.

*Query-conditional (the unbounded class, tested at identical volume):*
- **C6** **Training-free cross-encoder reranker**: rerank the retriever's top-12 by a cross-encoder and inject exactly the top 4. No outcome supervision, no training on task data, identical k. This is the boldest test in the paper: an untrained conditional policy against C3, an oracle static policy given unlimited outcome supervision.
- **C5** Learned conditional gate: gradient-boosted scorer over (query embedding, item embedding, cross-encoder relevance, retrieval rank, item length/type) trained on Phase-1+Phase-2 outcomes; at inference it scores the top-12 and admits above a threshold calibrated so the *mean* admitted count equals 4. Zero extra rollouts at inference.

*Volume controls:*
- **C7** Fixed-k budget tuning: no curation, k tuned on a 600-episode dev split.
- **C0′** Null replicate: C0 re-run under a different seed schedule.

*Headline comparisons.* C6 vs {C1, C3, C4, C9, C10}: does a training-free conditional policy beat every static policy including the oracle and the search? C1/C9/C10 vs C2: do published write-time signals beat random removal at matched volume? C3 vs C2: the ceiling on static item curation. C4 vs C3: is the ceiling a property of the class rather than the search? C5/C6 vs C7: is any of this a volume effect?

**PHASE 4 — PROXY AUDIT (120 verification replays, otherwise no rollouts).** Correlate against both the Phase-2 item main-effect posterior *and* the Phase-1 configuration×query interaction magnitude: A-MAC's composite and each of its five factors, judge quality, an EDV-style verification replay outcome, contradiction flag, SAGE novelty, retrieval frequency, item length, abstractness. Spearman with bootstrap CIs, plus AUC for identifying reliably-negative items. Two questions: do published signals predict the stable component, and does any predict *conditional* value — which would be a positive finding for that family and a route to a better read-time gate.

**BASELINE FIDELITY — PRE-REGISTERED, NO ESCAPE HATCH.** Each reimplemented method (A-MAC, judge prune, sequential editor, GEPA search, EDV replay) is tuned on a dev split with a hard 6-hour engineering cap each and a pre-stated fidelity check: it must reproduce the *direction* of its published end-to-end effect on dev. Reviewers correctly flagged the previous version's plan to exclude non-reproducing baselines as a way of quietly deleting disconfirming evidence. We therefore commit in advance: **every baseline enters the analysis and the refutation set regardless of fidelity outcome**, its fidelity result is reported in the main table, and a fidelity failure is reported as *itself informative* (consistent with our own thesis that write-time signals are weak) rather than as grounds for removal. Where public code exists we use it.

**SECONDARY MODEL (Llama-3.1-8B; 3,200 episodes).** Phase-1 dense design only, reduced: 100 instances × 8 configurations × 4 seeds (2 fit / 2 eval). Reports R1, R2, and the R3 ordering. Directional; MDE ~7 points on the conditional gain, stated as such. Its job is to show the sign and ordering of the static-vs-conditional gap is not a 14B artifact.

**STAGING AND GRACEFUL DEGRADATION.** Phases run in order 0→1→2→3→4. Phase 1 alone is a publishable result (the variance decomposition plus the P1/P2/P3 contrast). If engineering on Phase 3 overruns, conditions are dropped in this pre-stated priority order from the bottom: C10, C9, C5, C4, C7 — never C1, C2, C3, C6, which are the four that decide the audit.

**COMPUTE ARITHMETIC.** 700 (Phase 0) + 10,800 (Phase 1 + refs) + 2,400 (Phase 2) + 7,800 (Phase 3, incl. 2 random draws, null replicate, k-tuning dev) + 1,200 (GEPA search) + 120 (EDV replays) + 3,200 (8B) ≈ 26,200 episodes. Each episode ≤8 model calls, ~900 generated tokens plus ~12k prefill. Qwen2.5-14B on 2×A100 (TP=2), ≥1,500 tok/s per replica, two replicas ≥3,000 tok/s → ~3 episodes/s; discount 3× for tool latency, retries, scheduling → ~4,000 episodes/hour → ~7 GPU-hours of pure inference. Budgeting 3× for development plus one full re-run: under 3 days of node time. Engineering, budgeted separately: 6-hour cap per reimplemented baseline (5 baselines = ~1 developer-week), which is the cost the previous version failed to account for. API: 400 distillation calls + ~120 items × 4 API-side scores + ~400 sequential-editor calls + ~60 long-context GEPA reflections ≈ $170, hard cap $200. Outcome scoring is F1/EM, so no judging spend.
Baselines and Ablations:
**BASELINES THAT COULD WIN AND WOULD REFUTE THE CENTRAL CLAIM.**
(i) **P1 (best constant configuration) gaining ≥5 points over P0.** A fixed good package transfers across queries; the policy-class bound is wrong. This is the cleanest refutation and it is measured with ±2.5-point precision.
(ii) **C4 (GEPA static demonstration search) beating C5/C6.** A strong reflective optimizer breaks the static ceiling, so the ceiling was an artifact of our configuration pool or of weak static estimation, not of staticness. This is the baseline we consider most dangerous, and it is deliberately given the track's own best method.
(iii) **C3 (set-level oracle static prune) beating C2 by >3 points.** Static item curation works when you can estimate well; the field's problem is estimation, not conditionality — a more optimistic and equally publishable finding, and the one that would vindicate arXiv:2603.02473's reading over ours.
(iv) **C1 (faithful A-MAC), C9 (judge), or C10 (sequential editor) beating C2 by >3 points.** The published write-time signal carries real transferable information; reported as vindication of that family.
(v) **C7 (fixed-k tuning) matching C5 and C6.** The conditional advantage is a volume effect.
(vi) **P2 (feature-only conditional) failing to beat P1** while P3 succeeds. Conditional headroom exists but is not accessible from features; the honest conclusion is then much weaker and we say so (branch C below).
(vii) The matched-pair LOO estimator disagreeing sharply with the Phase-2 datamodel: item effects are an estimator artifact.

**CONTROLS AND ABLATIONS THAT CARRY THE MECHANISM.**
- *Matched-volume random removal (C2, 2 draws)* holds bank size and injected-token statistics fixed and removes only the identification signal. C1−C2, C9−C2, C10−C2 are exactly the value of the curation decision. Absent, as far as our searches found, from every curation paper — including from arXiv:2603.02473, whose write strategies also differ in item length and therefore in injected volume.
- *Fixed k=4 across all Phase-1 conditions* is what separates our account from "injection volume is the only lever." The volume account predicts the conditional selector gains nothing at fixed k; we predict ≥5.
- *P1/P2 nesting*: same estimator, same training data, same k, differing only by query-feature interaction terms. This is what makes the result a policy-class statement rather than a comparison of two unrelated systems.
- *Within-cell seed replication* identifies decoding noise non-parametrically, so "interaction dominates" cannot be an aliasing artifact.
- *Shuffled-configuration placebo*: permute configuration labels within instance, refit P1 and P2, recompute. P2−P1 must exceed the 95th percentile of this null.
- *Training-free vs trained conditional (C6 vs C5)*: isolates whether the conditional advantage requires outcome supervision. If C6 ≈ C5, conditionality — not learning — is the operative variable, which is the strongest form of the claim.
- *Coverage ablation*: Phase-2 reliability statistics recomputed on items with ≥60 appearances.
- *Injected-token accounting*: per-episode injected token counts reported for every Phase-3 condition, since C5 matches k only in expectation.
Falsifiable Predictions:
Pre-registered. Primary predictions are those the design can resolve at stated power; secondary ones are labelled underpowered.

**PRIMARY.**
- **F1 (the ceiling).** P1 − P0 ≤ **2 points** with a 95% CI excluding 5. The best constant configuration, fitted leave-one-instance-out, is near-indistinguishable from random equal-volume selection.
- **F2 (the decisive contrast).** P2 − P1 ≥ **5 points**, significant by paired Wilcoxon over 200 instances and exceeding the shuffled-configuration placebo 95th percentile. Same training data, same estimator, same k; only the hypothesis class differs.
- **F3 (headroom exists).** P3 − P0 ≥ **8 points**, establishing that P2 is capturing part, not all, of a large conditional signal. Reported as an upper reference, not a claim about deployable methods.
- **F4 (variance structure).** Configuration×query interaction ≥ **3×** the configuration main effect in the non-parametric decomposition; configuration main effect < **20%** of explainable (non-seed) variance. Config-sensitivity fraction (R2) ≥ **35%** of instances.
- **F5 (the audit).** No static condition beats matched-volume random removal by more than 3 points: |C1−C2|, |C9−C2|, |C10−C2|, |C3−C2| all within ±3 with CIs covering zero. C3 is load-bearing — it means the *ceiling*, not the estimator, binds.
- **F6 (the boldest claim).** **C6, the training-free cross-encoder reranker with zero outcome supervision, beats C3, the oracle static prune fitted on unlimited probe data, by ≥3 points at identical k** — and beats C1, C4, C9, C10 as well. If true, no amount of write-time supervision buys what an untrained read-time policy gets for free.
- **F7 (not volume).** C5 and C6 both beat C7 (fixed-k tuning). C4 lands within 2 points of C3 and does not exceed C0+3: a strong reflective search confined to static selection hits the same bound as an oracle static prune.
- **F8 (proxy audit).** Every write-time proxy, including A-MAC's composite and each of its five factors, has |Spearman| < **0.25** with the Phase-2 item main-effect posterior and AUC < **0.65** for reliably-negative items; fewer than **10%** of items have a 95% credible interval excluding zero.

**SECONDARY (direction only, underpowered).**
- **F9.** On the 8B model, the P2 > P1 ordering holds with the same sign; magnitudes may differ.
- **F10.** At least one write-time proxy correlates better with *conditional* value magnitude than with the item main effect; if so we name it as the most promising read-time gating feature.

**REFUTATION CONDITIONS AND PRE-REGISTERED BRANCHES.**
- P1 − P0 ≥ 5 → static selection is not bounded; the central claim fails, and the "better-chosen write policy could work" reading of arXiv:2603.02473 is vindicated over ours.
- C3 − C2 > 3 → an oracle static prune works; the ceiling claim is wrong and the field's problem is estimation. Optimistic, publishable, and we report it as such.
- C4 > C5 and C4 > C6 → optimizer-driven static selection beats conditional selection; the constructive corollary fails even if F1–F5 hold.
- P3 − P0 < 4 → **branch B**: memory selection is inert at fixed volume and only injection volume matters, contradicting the entire selection literature and strengthening the track's prior volume finding. Both branches indict item-level curation; they differ in the recommendation, and we declare which branch we are in before interpreting anything else.
- P3 − P0 ≥ 8 but P2 − P1 < 2 → **branch C**: conditional headroom is real but not feature-accessible with our features. We report the ceiling plus a negative result on reachability and explicitly do not claim "read-time selection is unbounded." This is the branch we consider most likely to cost us the headline, and we name it in advance rather than leaving ourselves room to narrate around it.
- Any proxy with |Spearman| > 0.4 against stable item value → that curation family is validated; reported as such.

**WHAT CHANGES IF WE ARE RIGHT, SPECIFICALLY.** (a) Matched-volume random removal becomes a mandatory ablation in memory-curation papers; we name A-MAC, SAGE, Memory-R1, AutoManual and EDV as papers whose headline gains are currently not separable from bank shrinkage, and we perform that separation for A-MAC ourselves. (b) arXiv:2603.02473's "raw chunked storage matches expensive write-time curation" is reinterpreted: our volume accounting says the write-strategy span it measures is partly a token-count effect, and the correct conclusion is not "these three write strategies are equivalent" but "no write strategy can do much," which is a strictly stronger and differently actionable statement. (c) For the coupling question this track is about: a prompt optimizer should own the *instructions*, and the *demonstration slot must be filled at read time conditioned on the query* — a static demonstration set found by GEPA is bounded no matter the search budget (C4 vs C6), so GEPA-style demonstration search on tasks with high configuration×query interaction is a category error, not an under-tuned method.
Measurement and Noise Control:
**Three noise sources, handled separately.**

*(a) Decoding noise* is measured, not assumed: 6 seeds per (instance, configuration) cell give a direct within-cell estimate, subtracted before any interaction claim. This is why the decomposition is identifiable rather than a random-effects fit to sparse cells.

*(b) Selection noise.* P2 never sees the target instance at all (leave-one-instance-out), so it cannot be inflated by selection on the target's noise. P3 selects on fit seeds and scores on disjoint eval seeds, so it is a lower bound on outcome-informed conditional value. The shuffled-configuration placebo gives the null distribution of apparent conditional gain under no true conditionality; P2−P1 is read as nonzero only above its 95th percentile.

*(c) Evaluation noise.* Every Phase-3 held-out instance is run under every condition with the same seed schedule; all comparisons are within-instance. Primary test is a paired bootstrap on F1 differences, Holm-corrected across the condition family; exact McNemar on EM fix/break counts is reported alongside, because a null net delta hiding symmetric churn is a different finding from an inert intervention. C2 is averaged over 2 draws with across-draw spread as a reference band. C0′ re-runs C0 under a different seed schedule; no effect is claimed unless it exceeds the 95th percentile of that replicate's apparent-delta distribution — load-bearing given prior observations of 5–14 point re-scoring drift.

**Minimum detectable effects, stated before running, with the design's asymmetry made explicit.**
- *P1 − P0 (the ceiling).* P1 is a constant policy, so each candidate configuration's mean is estimated from 200 instances × 6 seeds = 1,200 episodes. With per-episode F1 SD ≈0.30, SE per configuration ≈0.009; the LOO best-of-8 contrast against the pool average has SE ≈0.012 → **95% CI ≈ ±2.5 points**. This is the strongest number in the paper and it is strong precisely because the null is about a constant.
- *P2 − P1 (the decisive contrast).* Paired over 200 instances on mean F1 across 3 eval seeds. Expected SD of paired differences ≈0.22 (roughly half the instances receive identical configurations from both policies, contributing exact zeros) → SE ≈0.0156 → **MDE ≈4.4 points** at 80% power, α=0.05. F2 predicts 5. A P2−P1 between 2 and 4.4 is declared inconclusive **in advance**.
- *Phase 3.* 600 paired instances on F1: SD of paired condition differences ≈0.20 → SE ≈0.008 → **MDE ≈2.3 points**; null bands in F5/F6 are set at ±3 to sit safely above it. On EM with McNemar, expected ~90 discordant pairs → MDE ≈4.3 points, reported as the secondary and more conservative test.
- *Phase 2 item posteriors.* ~70 binary observations/item → per-item detectable effect ≈±22 points, so F8's "fraction of items clearing a 95% bar" is estimated tightly even though individual items are not. With 120 items, Spearman CIs ≈±0.17: we can separate 0.25 from 0.5 but not 0.25 from 0.35, and proxy differences below 0.2 will not be interpreted.
- *Secondary 8B.* 100 instances × 2 eval seeds → MDE ≈7 points; ordering only, stated as directional.

**Bootstrap.** All variance components, the config-sensitivity fraction, and every R3 contrast get 10k instance-level bootstrap resamples; CIs are reported on all derived quantities including decomposition ratios.
Preprint Collision Check:
Grounded in the search just run; I state plainly where it hurts.

**CLOSEST WORK, AND A PARTIAL COLLISION: "Diagnosing Retrieval vs. Utilization Bottlenecks in LLM Agent Memory" (arXiv:2603.02473, 2026).** This is the most dangerous paper for us and it was not in our earlier search passes. It runs a 3×3 factorial of write strategy × retrieval method on LoCoMo and reports that retrieval spans 20 points while write strategy spans 3–8, with raw chunking matching expensive curation. **It collides on the directional conclusion.** We therefore no longer claim "read-time matters more than write-time" as a finding; we cite it as established and re-centre our contribution on four things it does not do. (1) *Volume confound*: its three write strategies produce systematically different item lengths and therefore different injected token counts, so the small write-side span it measures is not separable from a token-budget effect — our matched-volume random-removal control and fixed-k design are built exactly to break that confound, and C1-vs-C2 tests it directly on the curation family. (2) *Three points are not a ceiling*: comparing raw chunks, Mem0 extraction and MemGPT summarization tells you those three are close, not that the best possible query-agnostic policy is close to random; our P1 (LOO best constant configuration), C3 (set-level oracle prune given unlimited probe data), C4 (GEPA search) and C10 (sequential editor) bound the class from several directions. (3) *No variance decomposition and no seed replication*, so it cannot say whether the write-side span it observes is above its own noise floor, nor attribute the read-side span to item×query interaction rather than to retrieval recall. (4) *Different regime*: long conversational memory (LoCoMo) versus tool-agent multi-hop QA with a distilled experience bank. **Decidable disagreement**: its account leaves open that a better-chosen or oracle write-side policy recovers much of the headroom; ours says no query-agnostic policy can. C3 vs C2 and P1 vs P0 settle it. Net effect on this proposal: novelty of *direction* is reduced and we concede it; novelty of the *bound*, the *mechanism attribution* (conditionality vs volume), and the *control* is intact.

**Read-time method papers, adjacent, not collisions.** CMI (arXiv:2605.17641) reselects memories at read time by estimated performance change and explicitly notes that topically related memories can be misleading — this is the closest in spirit to our C5 gate, and it is a method paper with no ceiling measurement and no volume control; our C5 is best described as a cheap, rollout-free instance of the CMI family, which we say in the paper. MemArbiter (arXiv:2608.02113) arbitrates among banks at decision time. LazyMem (arXiv:2607.22690) names the same write-vs-read tension and answers it architecturally. MemAct (arXiv:2510.12635) RL-optimizes in-episode edits. The rate–distortion framing (arXiv:2607.08032) argues theoretically that the bottleneck is read-side. None measures a ceiling, decomposes variance, or holds injection volume fixed; collectively they show a 2026 consensus forming around our direction, which is why the bound and the control are the parts worth publishing.

**Audited targets, unchanged.** A-MAC (arXiv:2603.04549) remains the named target; we could retrieve title/venue only, not the abstract, so I cannot verify whether it reports cross-context score transfer. Under either resolution it is a target rather than a collision, because neither a transfer test nor an admission-control method contains a ceiling measurement or a matched-volume random-removal control. Memory-R1 (arXiv:2508.19828) is now reimplemented in prompted form as C10, addressing the objection that a single-shot admission oracle does not cover sequential write policies. SAGE, A-MemGuard, AutoManual, EDV, TOKI enter as Phase-4 proxies at no rollout cost.

**Citation I am retracting.** The previous version anchored its sharpest counter-prediction on MEMAUDIT (arXiv:2605.02199), a "package oracle" paper I could not re-verify in two subsequent search passes, and reviewers rightly flagged that a positioning claim resting on an unverifiable citation is a substantive weakness. **I have removed that anchor entirely.** The differential prediction now runs against arXiv:2603.02473, which is verified and current, and against the implicit assumption shared by the whole write-time family. A distinct MemAudit (arXiv:2605.23723) exists and concerns poisoned-memory auditing — a different failure mode (adversarial correctness, not benign utility structure) — and is cited as such.

**Residual risk, unresolved.** A matched-volume random-removal control appearing as an appendix ablation in a very recent curation preprint would blunt C1-vs-C2. None of the retrieved papers, across three search passes, contains one. The search's own gap statement matches ours: no retrieved paper measures an upper bound on what write-time curation alone can achieve at fixed injection volume on a frozen bank. The dense factorial policy-class contrast (P1 vs P2 vs P3), the non-parametric variance decomposition, and the training-free-conditional-beats-oracle-static result are unclaimed by anything found.
Risk Factors and Limitations:
1. **Novelty is now partly conceded.** arXiv:2603.02473 has already shown the direction. If a reviewer believes the direction was the whole contribution, this proposal is incremental. We are betting that the bound, the volume control, and the policy-class attribution are what the field actually needs, and we have made the claim sharp enough that it can be wrong in a specific way rather than merely unsurprising.
2. **Branch C is live and we named it.** If P3 shows large headroom but P2 cannot reach it from features, the title's second half is unsupported and the paper becomes "the static ceiling is real, and the conditional headroom is not yet reachable." That is a weaker paper, it is pre-registered, and we will not narrate around it.
3. **Configuration pool bounds both sides.** P1, P2 and P3 range over 8 rank patterns, not all 495 size-4 subsets of the top-12. Our conditional numbers are lower bounds; our static number is a ceiling *within the same pool*, so the comparison is fair, but a richer pool could raise the static ceiling somewhat. C3 (unrestricted set-level oracle over the full bank) and C4 (unrestricted reflective search) bound the static side without that restriction, which is why they are in the design.
4. **Power asymmetry, stated rather than hidden.** The ceiling claim (P1−P0, ±2.5) is far better powered than the conditional contrast (P2−P1, MDE ≈4.4). Effects between 2 and 4.4 points on the conditional side are inconclusive and pre-declared as such. Switching the primary metric to F1 was done for exactly this reason and is disclosed as a design choice, not presented as neutral.
5. **Scope.** One environment, one primary model, one bank from one distillation procedure. The 8B arm tests only the sign of the ordering. We cannot say whether procedural items in embodied environments are more query-universal than QA insights — plausibly they are, and that is the first follow-up. We refuse to launder an underpowered 250-instance ALFWorld arm into generality.
6. **Baseline fidelity, no longer an escape hatch.** Two reviewers flagged that "exclude non-reproducing baselines" could quietly delete disconfirming evidence. We now commit to including every baseline in the refutation set regardless of fidelity outcome, reporting fidelity in the main table, and treating a fidelity failure as itself evidence about how robust that method's signal is. Engineering is capped at 6 hours per baseline and budgeted explicitly (~1 developer-week total), which the previous version omitted.
7. **Mean-volume matching is not exact.** C5 matches k in expectation; C6 matches it exactly, which is one reason C6 rather than C5 carries the boldest prediction. C7 absorbs the residual volume explanation and per-episode injected-token counts are reported for every condition.
8. **Randomized injection in Phase 2 deviates from deployment retrieval**, so item main effects are marginal over a slightly different distribution. Mitigated by drawing only from the top-20 and by the matched-pair LOO agreement check. Phase 1, which carries the decisive claim, draws from the retriever's own top-12 at deployment volume and does not have this problem.
9. **What I refused, and why.** (a) *Cutting the GEPA static search* (reviewer 1). Refused: without it, "the ceiling is a property of the policy class, not the search budget" is untested, and that is the claim. It is instead made cheaper (1,200 search episodes) and placed low in the drop-priority list only after the four audit-critical conditions. (b) *A trained RL admission controller* (reviewers 1 and 3). Refused as an RL training effort, but the substantive objection — that sequential ADD/DELETE over episode history is not covered by a cross-sectional admission oracle — is conceded and answered by C10, a prompted sequential bank editor, plus by making C3 a *set-level* rather than marginal oracle. What remains genuinely uncovered is a write policy that changes bank composition *over time under distribution shift*; we state that as out of scope. (c) *A faithful MemAct RL reimplementation* (reviewer 3). Refused: we deliberately use weaker conditional policies than MemAct's, so the ordering claim is conservative — if even a training-free reranker clears the static ceiling, the class ordering does not depend on the strongest read-time method existing. (d) *Reframing away from the P1/P2 contrast toward the variance decomposition alone* (reviewer 3's suggested fix). Partially refused: we kept the contrast as the headline but rebuilt it, replacing the outcome-informed oracle with a feature-only leave-one-instance-out policy that has no access to the target instance, which is what the reviewer's objection actually demanded. The oracle survives only as a labelled upper reference.
10. The payload is a bound on a policy class that a fast-growing literature depends on, so its value rests entirely on measurement strength. The placebo permutation, the leave-one-instance-out fitting of both P1 and P2, the matched-volume random-removal control, the null replicate, and the pre-stated MDEs are load-bearing and non-negotiable in the budget.

Name: substitutes_not_complements
Title: Substitutes, Not Complements: Clause-Level Evidence That Optimized Instructions Shrink an Agent's Useful Memory-Injection Budget
Short Hypothesis: Prompt-optimized instructions and retrieved episodic memory carry overlapping procedural information, so their combination is sub-additive: the accuracy-optimal injection budget k* falls from the high-k regime (4–8 items) under a minimal instruction to the low-k regime (0–2 items) under an instruction that contains the task's procedural clauses, and the harm is *relational* — deleting the specific instruction clause that a memory item duplicates restores that item's marginal value, while deleting a length-matched unrelated clause does not.
Related Work:
Two literatures bracket this question and neither asks it.

*Prompt optimization.* MIPROv2 (Opsahl-Ong et al., EMNLP 2024) is the closest technical relative: it formalizes prompt = instructions + demonstrations and jointly searches both. But it fixes a maximum demonstration count as a hyperparameter, draws demonstrations from bootstrapped training data rather than an evolving self-edited bank, and never reports an interaction between instruction quality and shot count. GEPA-style reflective evolution optimizes instruction text and treats the demonstration slot as separate and static.

*Agent memory.* ExpeL and Reflexion accumulate distilled experience and inject a fixed top-k. Recent work documents negative transfer as competition among experiences under a limited context window (arXiv:2604.27003), treats retrieval as risk-sensitive control (arXiv:2604.27283), and attributes memory failures to irrelevant retrieval (arXiv:2603.02473). ReasoningBank-style systems curate the bank at *write* time (contradiction pruning, deduplication). All of these hold the instruction fixed and treat memory quality as a property of the item, not of the (instruction, item) pair.

*Injection count as an ablation.* "On the Structural Memory of LLM Agents" (arXiv:2412.15266) ablates retrieved-memory count K and finds plateaus (≈77% flat across K on HotpotQA); RAVEN (arXiv:2308.07922) reports an upper limit on useful in-context examples; Coupling Retrieval and Meta-Learning (2019) notes excessive retrieved examples introduce noise. These establish that an optimal k exists — but all vary k with the prompt held fixed, which is exactly the axis we cross.

*RAG context filtering and compression.* FILCO-style context filtering, RECOMP-style compression, lost-in-the-middle dilution studies, MMR-based diverse retrieval, and chunk-level redundancy filtering (arXiv:2604.24334) all operationalize "gate retrieved content by redundancy" and "less context can be better". Every one of these measures redundancy either *among retrieved items* or *against the query*, never against the instruction, and every one treats the fix as compression rather than as a statement about where procedural knowledge should live. We therefore instantiate both MMR gating and RECOMP-style compression as first-class competing arms, so instruction-conditioned redundancy must earn its keep against the older and simpler ideas.

*Closest by causal structure.* MemMachine (arXiv:2604.04853) reports that prompt design and model choice must be co-optimized with retrieval and that this advantage persists across retrieval depths — i.e., prompt choice changes retrieval's marginal value. It does not frame this as substitution, does not estimate k* as a function of instruction content, and does not test the mechanism causally. Both reviewers named it as the nearest neighbour and as the reason our delta must be mechanism, not observation; the clause-knockout experiment (E4) is our answer to that.
Abstract:
Agent frameworks stack a self-editing experience memory on top of an automatic prompt optimizer and report end-to-end gains without asking how the two components interact. Pilot measurements motivating this work show that (i) injecting a full retrieved memory bank fixed zero test items and broke six to seven (McNemar p<0.05, replicated), (ii) reducing injection from seven items to three eliminated the harm from the *same* bank, making injection volume the causal lever, and (iii) re-scoring the same candidate moved the headline metric by 0.05–0.14, so most published deltas in this area sit under the noise floor. We propose one explanatory hypothesis that ties these together: optimized instructions and retrieved experience are informational *substitutes*. An instruction that already states a procedural regularity leaves a memory item encoding that same regularity no marginal information but a full share of the interference cost, so the accuracy-optimal injection budget shrinks as the instruction absorbs procedure.

The design is built around one causal test rather than a correlational one. We decompose a GEPA-evolved instruction into procedural clauses and build a graded ladder (minimal → half the clauses → full evolved instruction, plus a hand-written strong instruction that contains no optimizer output). The primary grid crosses this ladder with five injection budgets on one multi-hop QA agent and one 7B open model, item-paired on a fixed set of 800 items, and pre-registers only the *regime-level* claim (argmax-k moves from {4,8} to {0,1,2}) and the monotone ordering of the k-slope. The mechanism is then decided by a clause-knockout difference-in-differences: for each query we inject the single retrieved item that most duplicates a specific clause, and compare deleting *that* clause against deleting a length-matched unrelated clause. Substitution predicts the item recovers value only under the targeted knockout; a ceiling/saturation effect or any global property of the optimized instruction predicts no difference. Length-matched neutral padding (dilution), foreign-instruction redundancy (item-intrinsic quality), MMR inter-item redundancy, RECOMP-style compression, ReasoningBank-style write-time curation, and a joint (instruction, k) optimizer are the competing explanations we run against. Powered replications on a second model family and a second QA task are conditional on the primary result. Full plan: 76 paired evaluation passes ≈ 182k model generations plus 6 optimizer runs ≈ 1.5 GPU-days on one 4×A100 node, and ≈$70 of frontier API.
Experiments:
Everything below fits one node (4×A100 80GB, vLLM, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) and ≈$70 of frontier API. Tier 3 runs only if Tiers 1–2 come out positive.

**Shared setup.** Task: multi-hop QA (HotpotQA distractor, 2-hop ReAct-lite agent with a fixed retrieval tool; ~3 model calls per episode). Memory: ExpeL-style bank distilled from 500 training episodes (per-episode insight + trajectory summary), dense retrieval. Evaluation: one fixed set of n=800 held-out items, identical items and identical decoding seeds in every cell (greedy decoding for all grids; seeds varied only for the noise floor). Metric: answer EM/F1 (no judge needed for grading), with fixes and breaks always reported separately against the paired k=0 cell of the same instruction.

**Instruction ladder (constructed once, offline).** Run GEPA (memory disabled) with 3 seeds → I3-s1..s3. Decompose I3-s1 into K≈6–8 atomic procedural clauses with a frontier model, verified by hand. Ladder levels:
- I0 = minimal task statement.
- I1a, I1b = I0 + two disjoint halves of I3-s1's clauses (controls for "amount of procedure" while holding source constant).
- I3-s1..s3 = full evolved instructions.
- I_H = a hand-written strong instruction of comparable length written before seeing any results, containing no optimizer output. This is reviewer 1's requested control for GEPA-specific artifacts.

**Tier 1 — E1: the grid that decides the claim (25 passes).** k ∈ {0,1,2,4,8} for I0 and I3-s1 (10 passes); k ∈ {0,2,8} for I1a, I1b, I3-s2, I3-s3, I_H (15 passes). Pre-registered primary analysis: mixed-effects logistic regression on per-item correctness, item random intercept, instruction random intercept (seeds nested), fixed effects for instruction level, log(k+1), and their interaction; the hypothesis predicts a negative interaction. Secondary: ordered contrast on the k-slope across I0 → I1(pooled) → I3(pooled) (monotone trend test), and per-cell McNemar contrasts vs. that instruction's k=0 cell, Holm-corrected. **Gate:** I3 at k=0 must beat I0 at k=0 by more than the null-replicate floor, otherwise the grid is uninformative and that is the reported result.

**Tier 1 — E2: dilution placebo (4 passes).** Injected items replaced by topically plausible, task-irrelevant text at token counts matched to k=2 and k=8, for I0 and I3-s1. If padding reproduces the harm curve, substitution is refuted and the corrected finding is "memory harm is context dilution".

**Tier 1 — E3: noise floor (12 passes).** 3 representative cells × 4 replicate evaluations differing only in decoding seed; one identical replicate is relabelled as a "treatment" to measure the apparent effect produced by nothing.

**Tier 2 — E4: clause knockout, the causal mechanism test (6 passes).** For each of the 800 queries, score every top-8 retrieved item against every clause of I3-s1 (embedding cosine over clause text + NLI entailment), and select the item m* with the highest redundancy against a single clause c(m*). Conditions, with m* held fixed within query:
- A: I3-s1 full, m* injected. B: I3-s1 minus c(m*) ("targeted knockout"), m* injected. C: I3-s1 minus c′ ("placebo knockout"), m* injected, where c′ is a length-matched clause that no item retrieved for this query duplicates.
- Plus the three matched no-item cells (A0, B0, C0) needed to compute each item's marginal value.
Analysis: difference-in-differences on per-item correctness, (B−B0) − (A−A0) versus (C−C0) − (A−A0), permutation test over items. Substitution predicts the targeted knockout restores m*'s value strictly more than the placebo knockout. **This is the ceiling/saturation killer:** both knockouts have near-identical global instruction quality (we verify B0 vs. C0 are indistinguishable within the noise floor and report that check), so any explanation that appeals to "I3 is already near ceiling" or "optimized instructions are just longer/more specific" predicts a null DiD.

**Tier 2 — E5: item-level predictor and its placebos (5 passes).** Single-item injections spanning the redundancy range: for each query, the median-R and min-R items from its top-8, under I3-s1 (2 passes) and under I0 (3 passes: max-R, median-R, min-R), reusing E4's arm A as the I3/max-R cell → 4,000 (query, item) observations. Regression of paired outcome change on R(I,m), controlling for retrieval score, item token length, item correctness, and **inter-item (MMR) redundancy**. Placebos computed offline on the same data: R against a *foreign task's* optimized instruction (item-intrinsic control) and R against I0 while running under I3 and vice versa (relational control). A frontier judge ("does the instruction already tell the agent what this item tells it?", 0–4) validates the two local scorers on a 400-pair subsample only (≈$10); it is never used at scale.

**Tier 2 — E6: is substitution an artifact of the two-stage design? (6 passes, 2 optimizer runs).** (a) One GEPA run whose candidate is the pair (instruction, k), k ∈ {0,2,8}, scored on the optimizer's own validation minibatches; report the selected k and evaluate the selected pair plus its two off-k variants held out (3 passes). (b) I_co = an instruction evolved with memory active at k=8 (1 seed), evaluated at k ∈ {0,2,8} (3 passes). If k* stays small even for an instruction co-adapted to a large context, the two-stage-artifact explanation is dead.

**Tier 3 (conditional) — E7: powered replications (12 passes).** Same protocol, n=800 paired, k ∈ {0,2,8} × {I0, I3-s1}: (a) second model family, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, same task; (b) second task, MuSiQue-2hop, same model and harness. Both are powered for the regime-level claim (MDE ≈2.5 points paired), not direction-only tokens. These replace the previously proposed ALFWorld arm, which was both expensive and underpowered.

**Tier 3 (conditional) — E8: redundancy-gated injection (RGI) versus the named alternatives (6 passes).** RGI admits retrieved items in retrieval-score order, skipping any with R(I,m) > τ (τ calibrated on a 200-item validation split), with a per-query cumulative-novelty cap. Competitors at matched or smaller token budgets: best validation-tuned fixed k; retrieval-score thresholding; MMR gating; **RECOMP-style compression** (items summarized to the same token budget rather than dropped — reviewer 2's named baseline); **ReasoningBank-style write-time curation** (contradiction pruning + deduplication of the bank, one frontier-API pass, ≈$5 — reviewer 1's named baseline); token-matched random budget.

**Resource arithmetic.** One paired pass = 800 items × ~3 model calls ≈ 2,400 generations. Passes: Tier 1 = 25+4+12 = 41; Tier 2 = 6+5+6 = 17; Tier 3 = 12+6 = 18. Total 76 passes ≈ 182k generations ≈ 46M decoded and ≈550M prefilled tokens; with vLLM prefix caching (instruction and memory prefixes shared within a cell) ≈10 GPU-hours of throughput, budgeted at ≤48 h wall clock with retries and the Llama serving switch. Optimizer: 6 GEPA runs (3 I3 seeds, 1 joint, 1 co-adapted, 1 spare) × ~1,500 rollouts × 3 calls ≈ 27k generations ≈ 2 h. Total ≈1.5 GPU-days on the single node. API: 6 optimizer runs × ~100 reflection calls × ~5k tokens ≈ $30–50; clause decomposition ≈ $2; judge validation 400 pairs ≈ $10; bank curation ≈ $5. Total ≈ $50–70.
Baselines and Ablations:
Baselines that could plausibly beat us:
1. **Validation-tuned fixed k** — the honest competitor. If RGI cannot beat a well-tuned fixed k=1 or 2, the practical claim fails; the scientific interaction and mechanism claims can still stand and we will say so explicitly.
